note.value: THE KING'S REPLY, WINDSOR, 28 DEC., 1.55. P.M.

text.p: On Lt. Aylesford's having accepted the office of Captain of the Yeomen of the Guards, I shall make no objection to Mr Pitt's acquainting Lt. Gower that Lt. Galloway will be appointed to the vacancy this will occasion in my Bedchamber, and I shall send notice to Lt. Weymouth to send the proper information to Lt. Galloway, who, till he receives that, cannot be presented to me. I trust Mr Pitt will appoint Lt. Clarendon, and Lt. de Ferrars to attend on Wednesday to receive their employments, as also Lt. Aylesford if he is in town, and Lt. Tankerville. I perfectly approve of Lt. Walsingham being one of the Vice-Treasurers of Ireland and Mr Pitt's acquainting him that it is by my direction he notifies this to him, who also may be presented on Wednesday. The Admiralty Commission has not yet been with me; if Mr Pitt is not ready with a commoner, why does he not find some peer who would hold it till it may be convenient otherwise to fill it up? Till then Lt. Keppel's Admiralty Board continues and Lt. Howe is really out of office.

As to Ireland I like the idea thrown out on Friday by Mr Pitt of the propriety of Lt. Cornwallis holding that office; though I doubt his accepting of it, I do not think that a reason Mr Pitt should not attempt it; Lt. Sydney is a good channel to find out whether it would succeed.

I cannot sufficiently express to your Majesty how much I felt on receiving your last gracious letter. The situation in which your Majesty has just been was most critical, and required the greatest firmness to extricate yourself out of it, though I confess that from the manner in which the members of the late Administration entered into office one could easily foresee that power was their only object, and that they would stick at nothing to fix that power upon a firm and sure bottom. Their attempt was most daring, as it was striking at the very roots of the Constitution. Happy, however, it is that they have miscarried and that they have themselves shown openly to the whole nation how little confidence was to be placed in their repeated declarations. Your Majesty's conduct through the whole of this critical affair will have convinced every true lover of his country how much you are resolved that the Constitution shall not be infringed in any part whatsoever, and how much you consider the interest of the nation as your own. Indeed, everything depended upon your firmness, and I have no doubt but that with that fortitude of mind which your Majesty has shown upon this as well as upon many other occasions, and which it must ever be the most ardent wish of every one who is really attached to your person and to the nation that your Majesty should persevere in, you will at last be able to settle everything again upon a sure and solid foundation. This whole affair must probably have cost your Majesty many disagreeable moments and in great measure have affected your health, but I hope you will soon recover yourself. I am sorry my brother so far forgot himself as to give his vote upon this occasion; it is, however, very lucky that he seems, by the excuses he thought proper to make to your Majesty, convinced of his error, and I hope that this may pave the way to put an end to those unhappy differences which have for some time subsisted.

As your Majesty's time is so much taken up I shall not trespass longer upon it. I shall therefore conclude with returning my most humble thanks to your Majesty for the trouble you have given yourself in sending me so exact an account of the whole of this affair. May I at the same time add my congratulations upon the new year, and that it may pass over with more satisfaction than the last. P.S. After having wrote thus far I received your Majesty's gracious letter of the 23d. Permit me, Sir, to return you my most sincere thanks for it. I have already
said enough on this subject in my letter; I shall therefore not touch upon it again. May I trouble your Majesty to give my duty to the Queen and to acquaint her that I shall do myself the honour of writing to her by the next post, having been too much hurried today to be able to send my letter by this courier. I should not have ventured to have sent this letter after what your Majesty was pleased to mention in your last, had it not been for the opportunity which presents itself of the quarterly courier who has my particular orders to deliver this into your own hands.

Mr. Drummond may be surprised to receive this from me, but being under the necessity of raising a sum of twenty four thousand pounds, and choosing to deal with a gentleman rather than addressing myself through others to the common sort of moneyed men, and not thinking it fair to have sent abruptly to Mr. Drummond and make my application to him, I now write that he may consider of it before I send to see him. What has occurred to me is that I am willing to give such a bond as Mr. Drummond may think necessary, with an assurance of repaying three thousand pounds every three months and of giving five per cent for the money.

By the account I settled with Lord North when he quited the Treasury he stated that I owed thirteen thousand pounds to Mr. Drummond, of which I have payed through the hands of Lord Brudenel seven thousand pounds; the other six is still owing, and was kept back at the desire of Lord North, he having a personal account to settle with Mr. Drummond, on which subject I fear he has not
acted very explicitly. He has never explained this as yet; this indeed has the more made me on the present occasion not wish to employ a middle person, consequently the bond must be for thirty thousand pounds at five per cent; three thousand pounds to be repaid every three months, and in case any accident should happen to me, I am willing that a sum of money I have in the stocks belonging to my German dominions shall be a colateral security that Mr. Drummond may run no hazard.

By your letter of the 2d of last month I see by the good management of Major General de Bude` he has been able to assist you in discharging some debts you have made. I cannot too strongly set before your eyes that if you permit yourself to indulge every foolish idea you must be wretched all your life, for with thirteen children I can but with the greatest care make both ends meet and am not in a situation to be paying their debts if they contract any, and to anyone that has either the sentiments of common honesty or delicacy, without the nicer feelings which every gentleman ought to possess, the situation of not paying what is due is a very unpleasant sensation. In you I fear that vanity which has been too predominant in your character has occasioned this, but I hope for the future you will be wiser. I cannot conclude without saying that I wish you had profited as much by my sending you to Hanover as Frederick has the commendation of all ranks of people. His civility and propriety are remarked by all that come from thence, but I am sorry to say your manners are still compared, as I too well saw when you returned from America, to the frequenters of the forecastle, and your love of improper company, particularly of some ill behaved Englishmen that have been at Hanover. This intelligence does not come from any that attend you, and therefore I have not hinted to Bude` that I know this, but you may easily believe nothing
can pass at Hanover that I am not acquainted with. I mention this that you may reflect on your conduct and consider that a Prince is to be an example to others, that by the propriety of your conduct I can alone with justice to my country advance you in your profession; that the levity which was natural in a boy must ill become you now that when you return to sea you must be the Prince, the gentleman and the officer, which requires ideas I fear as yet you have not turned your mind to. I have here given you the advice of an affectionate father. It is not by promises I am to be lulled; I shall by your future conduct watch whether my advice takes any real effect and then you will ever find me

As the time approaches in which I always understood it to be your Majesty's intention that I should return to my professional duty at sea I beg leave thus early to solicit your Majesty's attention to that object, trusting that you will not impute my doing so to any other cause than the strong desire I have to gain experience & distinguish myself in the line of service which you have been pleased to place me in.

I do not, Sir, presume to offer to your Majesty any ideas relative to my destination & mode of service, relying upon your better judgment & paternal care towards me in these prospects; nevertheless, if the East Indies should occur to your Majesty as an eligible station for me, & you should at the same time be deterred from choosing it under an apprehension that it would be disagreeable to me, I beg leave in that case to assure your Majesty that I have no dislike or objection whatever to serve in the East Indies: on the contrary I should most readily & cheerfully embark for a station which has at all times been regarded as one of the best schools for the forming of a naval officer.

note.value: 192 THE KING TO THE PRINCE OF WALES

text.p: The Prince of Wales is sufficiently aware that his letter of the 14th of March is not deemed by me a satisfactory or suitable answer to my proposal of the 13th. It contains a paper dated the 27th of October 1784, entitled, an estimate of debts and engagements; the first being debts already contracted, amounting to £58,443. The second, of debts he is still resolved to contract, amounting to £63,850; in all, £122,293. This paper it should seem was drawn out in consequence of the Prince's order to Colonel Hotham of the 17th of September, of which he gave me notice by Lord Southampton on that day.

On the 5th of January the Prince of Wales had represented the gross amount of his debts to be £150,000 without farther explanation. By way of farther explanation the above mentioned paper is sent to me, with a note subjoined to it of money borrowed on the 22d of December 1784 amounting to £25,000, which, added to the former sums, make £147,293. The paper does not purport an account of the present debts, nor even mention the names of the creditors, the conditions of loan, or other particulars respecting the nature of his engagements, for which in the last article of £15,000 Colonel Hotham makes this apology, that H.R.H. has not yet been pleased to inform him thereof . In short, it corresponds so little with the avowed
object of my enquiry, that these particulars would not be worth observing, if they did not derive some importance from an assertion in the Prince of Wales's letter of the 23d of March that every thing which either he or Colonel Hotham knows concerning every debt has already been submitted to me .

That letter proceeds to insist on the impossibility of making any abatement of his income, as it is with the greatest difficulty that he is able to go on with it at present , and infers from my having stated to him the necessity of his adopting some plan of retrenchment, that I find myself unable to assist him so far as I could wish ; and thereupon declines all farther communication upon this business, and concludes with a menace to run away from his situation, in direct defiance of the solemn injunction I have laid upon him not to leave the Realm without my express permission. The immediate consequences of executing such a threat, if that step were really taken, both to the Prince himself and to any person who might bear a part in it, make it of some importance that whatever has passed in this correspondence should be rightly understood.

I have hitherto said nothing either of my power or intention to assist in delivering the Prince of Wales from the embarrassments into which he is daily drawing himself; nor of the proportions in which his present means ought to be applied to that end: but I have frequently said, and I now repeat that my concurrence in any plan for that purpose, must depend on its being formed with sufficient regard both to his honour and mine. It is in my judgement essential to both that considerable expense should not either now or hereafter be entailed on the public on this account; that some scheme of economy should be settled for reducing his expense within a certain measure; and that the observance of it should be secured as far as the nature of the occasion will permit.

To reform the profusion of his present expenditure, that expenditure and the management under which it has issued must be examined, the excesses in the one must be retrenched, the abuses in the other corrected, and a settled application of his income must be made to a measured rate of necessary expense. This must be further secured by making his servants responsible in their several departments for their diligence and fidelity in the observance of it. To this end their accounts should be submitted to due examination from time to time. That no future debts may be contracted, the examination and payment of the present debts should be ordered, as to cut off all temptation to borrow, or lend in an improper manner. This or some other plan equally adapted to the avowed principle upon which alone I can ever interpose, must be adopted; for it is extremely obvious that to advance £150,000 and leave things as they are, would only occasion the same situation a year or two hence, with additional reproach to the wisdom and honour of all parties concerned.

To look into the detail of pocket expenses is no part of this object, on the other hand it is plain that no articles material to the avowed principle of this enquiry, can be buried under loose denominations, with defeating altogether the object proposed.

note.value: 195 THE DUKE OF YORK TO THE KING

text.p: As the last letter, which I had the honour of writing to your Majesty went by the post, I did not think it safe to answer many parts of your last gracious letter. Permit me therefore, Sir, to take this opportunity of repeating my most humble thanks for your goodness in permitting me to be entrusted in everything belonging to the military here. After having been informed of the general formation of the Krieges Kanzlei , the gentlemen have thought it best that I should go twice a week to the College itself, in order that I may be more au feet of the manner of treating the affairs than I could possibly be were I only to hear the report after their conclusion.

What your Majesty is pleased to say about the Emperor's projects is most exceedingly just. They are certainly more extensive even than one can imagine, and if not put a stop to at the very beginning it will be impossible to do it when they are come to maturity.

I have been desired by William to express to your Majesty how very sorry he is for having given you, Sir, occasion to be displeased with him, and how much it shall be his first care to behave himself in future in a more becoming manner; he certainly appears affected with your Majesty's last letter. But pardon me, Sir, if I add, that there never can be any real alteration for the better in him till he has been kept for some time under severe discipline, which alone can be done on board of ship, for his natural inclination for all kind of dissipation will make him, either here or indeed in any place by land, run into any society where he can form to himself only an idea of pleasure.

We have hopes of engaging a very good troop of German comedians here, at the head of which is Schroeder, who is without doubt the very best German actor that ever existed. It only depends upon your Majesty's being graciously pleased, in addition to what you at present give, to allow him the music and light. As for the music, it is only necessary to order that your Band, who have at present nothing to do, should play, and as for the lights it is a very trifling expense.
I will not trespass longer upon your Majesty's leisure...

The punctuality with which you have always performed every minutest part of your duty during the time I have had the pleasure of personally knowing you, added to your discretion and the attachment you have ever shown to the real good of my children, makes me pitch on you to acquaint the P. of Wales with what I should have done by word of mouth, had he not, when he came here to mention the affair of his separate Establishment, changed his mind, and from what I learnt from the Queen, begged her to thank me, declining doing it in person, least it might draw on a conversation which might embarrass him. I am not surprised he avoided it, as his conscience, if not entirely put to sleep, as well as his knowledge of my sentiments, must have made him expect that on such an occasion I should have uttered very homefelt truths. Now that the business is fully in train I desire you will acquaint him that not thinking it advisable to apply to Parliament for any further assistance than such as may enable me to allow fifty thousand pounds per annum which, with the revenue of Cornwall, will make his income twenty seven thousand more than the late King thought sufficient for me in a similar situation; which will, I am fully persuaded, enable him with proper attention and economy to live handsomely, but not with the shameful extravagance he has shown till now, which appears the stronger by an intimation he has sent me through the D. of Portland, that he has debts to the amount of above twenty nine thousand pounds, to which I might add what I gave him on a former very improper business. He must therefore recollect that this is the last time his debts can be paid, and that consequently he must live on the sum allotted, and that I do expect an assurance through you from him of his intentions to keep within bounds. What I mean to apply to Parliament for his debts and for fitting up his house, stables, and any other necessaries upon this occasion is a sum of sixty thousand pounds. I mean to let him have the use of the house my late mother inhabited in Pall Mall, but on condition that the premises be not damaged; particularly that the passage my mother granted to the late D. of York be not widened, and that he shall take all repairs, taxes, and the expenses of keeping the garden on himself; he must also find stables in town for his horses, and houses for his carriages, I having no room for them; besides an interference of separate servants is very inconvenient.

As to a country house I have none for him; besides, it would draw on so many additional expenses I think it best avoided; his apartment at Windsor shall always be kept ready to receive him, yet should he wish another, he must provide it himself; but I hear again repeat he must, if he means not to lose the good opinion of this nation, avoid debts.
I do not mean to propose any addition to his attendants except those of an inferior kind, which a separate house and table naturaly require.

Whenever he shall think it right to express to me the wish of marrying, then I shall look on myself authorized to apply to Parliament that his annual income may be increased to one hundred thousand pounds.

I cannot quit this subject without just saying that a plan must now be prepared under his inspection for the expenses of his house-keeping, stables, and Privy Purse, keeping back a sum for extraordinaries which should be exactly followed, or he will soon be obliged to retrench or do worse; now is the hour to put the whole on a proper footing; as to furnishing and repairing the house, buying or hiring stables, estimates should be first made, that the expense do not exceed the means of effecting them.

I cannot conclude without mentioning that I am convinced the P. of Wales on the smallest reflection must feel that I have little reason to approve of any part of his conduct for the last three years; that his neglect of every religious duty is notorious, his want of common civility to the Queen and me not less so, besides his total disobedience of every injunction I had given him, and which he in the presence of his brother and the gentlemen then about them both declared himself contented with.

I must hope he will now think it behoves him to take up a fresh line of conduct more worthy of his station, that he may regain the good opinion of men of religion, decency, and worth, and that a continuation of levity may not shorten his days, and make him too late repent of not having followed the advice of an affectionate though distressed parent.

Your Majesty's quarterly messenger Momentein arrived here on Friday last. I desired him to present to you my humble duty and to inform you that he found me extremely happy and extremely grateful to your Majesty's goodness for my being so.

I take the earliest opportunity to inform your Majesty that on Saturday last I went for the first time to the Guard, your Majesty's finest wood in the neighbourhood of Luneburg, to shoot. As the place was too distant from Luneburg for me to return home, I slept in a house belonging to your Majesty there. During our stay, Baron de Groat, whose country seat is very near the forest, invited me to dine with him on the Sunday, which invitation, with Mr. Wanghenheim's approbation, I accepted. We danced in the evening, and the Baron earnestly requested of me to sleep there that night, but as I imagined that might not meet with your Majesty's approbation, I refused his offer and returned home.

I hope your Majesty will not be displeased with my asking your permission to see the camp at Hanover this year. I sincerely hope that if your Majesty shall judge it proper to refuse my request, I shall not incur your displeasure from having asked it.

I humbly beg to recommend to your Majesty's gracious notice, Hawk, whom I find to be a most excellent, useful steady servant, and whom, if it should meet with your approbation, I should be extremely happy hereafter to have for myself. Had I but known his merits before I came here, I should have requested of your Majesty to have had him for my own servant, for Rymer, though a very honest, quiet, good mortal, is, I find, of very little use to me here; not that I mean at all to take from his merits by praising the other.
I must humbly beg of your Majesty to present my most respectful duty to the Queen and my most affectionate love to my sisters.

It was with the greatest sorrow that I heard from General Bude` of the melancholy illness of poor Elizabeth. From my own feelings upon this occasion, I can easily conceive what must have been your Majesty's anxiety & that of the Queen. I fear that so very immediately after the account of the unfortunate death of poor Prince George, this additional occasion of anxiety must have made the Queen extremely unhappy.

I flatter myself that your Majesty will graciously approve of my conduct and of my attention to my studies since my departure from England. I hope that with ardent endeavours to study my profession and follow every branch of instruction according to your orders, I shall in time become capable of acting in the station in which your Majesty may judge fit to place me. I have also endeavoured to advance as much as possible in the language, which I find not near so difficult as I had imagined.

I must humbly beg of your Majesty to present my most respectful duty to the Queen, and if I might presume to request it of your Majesty, my most affectionate love to my sisters who, I trust, will ever join me in prayer to Heaven for your happiness & that of the Queen.

As this is the first day I have had it in my power to write to your Majesty, I now take up my pen to return my most hearty & sincere thanks for the late honour conferred on me. How little I deserved it, I am fully sensible of; it shall be the utmost of my endeavours to follow the rules your Majesty laid down for me when your gracious intentions were first made known to me concerning my advancement in the service. I took the liberty of asking Lord Howe for the regulations he gave when he commanded a ship; after I have made a compilation of orders for the Pegasus I shall transmit them to Lord Howe & desire him to give me his opinion, & whenever any thing occurs unusual in the service, I shall always take the liberty of writing to his Lordship, as I am thoroughly acquainted with your Majesty's sentiments concerning Lord Howe. With respect to your Majesty's observation respecting my conduct towards the officers of the Pegasus, I am fully sensible of the necessity of keeping them at a proper distance without pride, & can with truth say they themselves know the propriety of this & will on their part adhere to it. They are all of a certain age & behave with great propriety. My cabin is the plainest in the service: the chairs are all of wood painted green. In my money matters I have begun & shall continue to keep
my accounts with regularity. The first fitting out is always expensive: I have endeavoured to keep to what will be only absolutely necessary.

I must once more return my thanks to your Majesty for my promotion. I feel that whilst in Germany my conduct was not such as to merit my parent's approbation. Now the case is very much altered: being in command I must pay regard to my behaviour, & show myself worthy of your Majesty's esteem, for which purpose the utmost endeavours of that person shall be exerted, who is, Sir

note.value: 315 THE DUKE OF YORK TO THE KING

text.p:
I take the opportunity of the quarterly messengers setting off this evening to acknowledge the receipt of your Majesty's gracious letter of the 14 which came safely to my hands this morning. What you are pleased to say about my brothers appears to me to be perfectly just. By the last letter which I received from Colonel Malhortie every thing seems to go on in the best manner possible, and Adolphus appears to have gained the hearts of every body at Gottingen. Colonel Wangenheim has informed me that he transmits to your Majesty according to your order the account of the debts which my brother Edward made during his stay at Lunebourg. As I am afraid that they will appear to your Majesty excessive I think it but justice to Wangenheim for me to assure you, Sir, that he never had the least knowledge of them, and indeed it would have been difficult for him or for any of the other gentlemen to have been acquainted with it as people were so very absurd as to give Edward credit to any amount that he pleased, and even to offer to lend him as much money as he wanted. So that till Wangenheim had your Majesty's order to get the list together of them towards their being paid, he could not form to himself even an idea about it. I take the liberty to enclose to your Majesty a report which Colonel True has drawn up concerning the new invented scaling ladder which has answered even beyond anybody's expectations. I have been desired by General Freytag just to hint to you, Sir, as the last firelocks which have been delivered out to the different Regiments have proved so bad that the Chancery of War and the Field Marechal have agreed to
have a new model made, if you would not take this opportunity to order the model which you have been pleased to approve of for the Light Infantry to be adopted.

It is now three years since I have been of age, and your Majesty's Minister Monsieur de Bussche has been so good as to assist me in managing the affairs of the Bishopric, without my having as yet ever made him any present. May I therefore now ask your Majesty's permission to do it? If this meets, Sir, with your approbation may I humbly beg your Majesty to acquaint him with it by a rescript, as it certainly will give him then much more pleasure to receive the permission unasked by himself, as he is not in the least informed of my intention.
I am afraid your Majesty will already be tired by this long letter. I shall therefore conclude...

Not having been told till after I wrote to your brothers of your having wrote to two of your sisters, I accused you of negligence, which has proved groundless. I therefore begin with explaining it as no one should be above confessing when they have been mistaken.

I am pleased with your expressing satisfaction at having seen the coat of mail of King George I, whose descendants cannot enough venerate him, for he was as honest, brave and just a man as ever was born; these are solid ingredients without which no character can be either respectable or amiable. I think I see strong seeds of these in you, which makes me add that I shall be

P.S. Considering how much your eldest sister loves you, would it not have been better that one of the others had remained without a letter from you than her? I am certain it hurts her though she has not said so.

Sir, I should not have troubled you with a letter this post but to inform you of a very disagreeable catastrophe that might have befell us but the great Creator of all things would not permit it. On Friday the 4th at 12 o'clock at night a fire broke out at a butcher's 4 doors from us opposite to Lichtenberg's. It raged violently, so much so that Linsingen, who has always his eyes about him, sent for some soldiers to go on the roof of our house with pales of water to hinder any spark from falling on our house. In one minute almost Hawk had got all the plate & papers packed up & ready to be carried out at the first notice. Brawn had everything in the wardrobe ready to take out. But at 3 the next morning it was near extinguished. There are 2 houses burnt down. All the times my brother & I were fast asleep, but Adolphus pretends he was awake but was so frightened as not to be able to speak. The dog that lays in my room hearing the cries barked, which awoke me. The next day I went over the 2 houses & the fire was not quite out then. There arrived yesterday another Englishman, Mr. Bathurst, a relation of Lord Bathurst's. Lord Dalrimple came & dined with us the other day. We have everything in plenty here but leather to make breeches, & what there is is horrid, not only the stuff but the workmanship.

Your Majesty will, I hope, graciously forgive me for not having sooner written after receiving your gracious letter of the 29th of August, but having nothing particular to inform your Majesty of, I wished to wait till such time as I could have the honour of telling you that I had been at Hammel. This tour I had long been very desirous of taking, as it is reckoned by many officers of great merit & distinction here to be one of the most complete works of modern fortification known in the world, and therefore extremely instructive for every officer who, a young beginner like me, is very desirous to learn his duty fundamentally so as to serve to your Majesty's approbation & his own honour. I therefore went to Hammel on Monday last, accompanied by Captn. Green, who had been previously there with his father, to render himself capable of explaining it to me. We were employed 4 hours in examining the whole of the fortifications of the fort with the Commander General Busche & the engineer Major Kunest, whose pains and trouble to explain every thing to me I cannot sufficiently acknowledge. After dinner I returned directly to Hanover, but on the road met with a disastre which might have been very fatal, but which I providentially escaped. The axle tree of our phaeton broke; I fell out of the carriage & was dragged above thirty paces by the horses, who galloped off with the pole & fore axle tree, but however I was so lucky as to escape with only bruises on the arm & thigh. I have taken the liberty
to mention this accident to your Majesty, that should it come to your ears by another quarter you might be acquainted with the reality of the fact.

May I presume to request of your Majesty to present my most humble duty to the Queen. I should have had the honour of writing to her by this post, but the accident on my right arm still gives me much pain, & I hope she will on that account graciously forgive my delaying it for a few days.
Should your Majesty observe any defect in the writing of this letter, I hope, Sir, that the same excuse will plead my apology.

note.value: 332 THE KING TO THE DUKE OF YORK

text.p:
My dear Frederick, I take the first leisure minute to answer your letter intimating a very natural wish to make your family a visit; however desirous you may be, it cannot exceed the joy I shall feel when I see you, but I must not let my inclinations decide where good reasons clearly show me I should be wrong. The conduct of your brother and the Party in whose hands he has unhappily thrown himself undoubtedly give every reason to expect this winter will be a pretty smart one. I know I can depend on your attachment and rectitude, therefore your conduct would be decided, for now a middle part is impossible; however I may be dissatisfied with your brother, the making a breach between
you is not my wish; your being absent keeps you with propriety out of the conflict. Another natural reason occurs from the present state of the Continent where a war seems not unlikely; in which case if you are there I shall certainly give you the command of my Electoral troops for that occasion. Military service must at present be your only object and you must be on the spot to see everything ready for such an event. Another observation occurs, that you could not be here in winter without my appointing a proper attendance for you; I am not in a situation to do that at present. Therefore rest assured, my dear Frederick, when I see the proper moment I shall not lose a day in reminding you how much I wish for your coming. As to the reason you give of wishing to learn the minutie of the Service, the Foot Guards is not the best school for that, as all the Officers of the Line who have come into those Corps very well know. I mentioned being anxious for your learning it merely as an inducement to your accepting of the command of the Hannoverian Guards; with a little information from our friend Grenville you may acquire it in your closet.

note.value: 355 THE DUKE OF YORK TO THE KING

text.p: I take the very earliest opportunity to acknowledge the receipt of your Majesty's very gracious letter of the 17, and to return you my most humble thanks for your great goodness in acquainting me with the time which you intend for my return home to England. It is not necessary I trust to express to you, Sir, the impatience with which I shall wait for the beginning of August and how happy it will make me to see your Majesty and the Queen again after so very long an absence. I am by no means fond of making professions, but I hope, Sir, you will permit me to assure you that it shall ever be my first care to act in such a manner as to meet with your approbation and to be deserving of that confidence and affection which your Majesty has been pleased upon all occasions to show towards me.

I shall therefore set out from hence the thirteenth of May for the Reviews at Potsdam, Berlin and Magdebourg, and on my return back mean to pass through Brunswick in order to take leave of the Duchess, so that I shall be here again on the thirtieth. On the 10th of June I shall go according to your Majesty's orders to the Camp at Luneburg and shall return here again about the 23. I do not then mean to leave this place except for a small excursion to take leave of my brothers at Gottingen till I set out upon my return home, which will be about the 21 or 22 of July, which by stopping four or five days to arrange every thing at Osnabruck,
and a day or two at different places which I shall want to see, will bring my arrival in England to about the 8 or 10 of August which I believe is exactly according to your Majesty's intentions.

Your Majesty will already be informed that in spite of all the Landgrave's declarations he has thought fit to obey the Decree of the Imperial Chamber and to withdraw his troops out of the country of Lip Schaumbourg. It is astonishing however, what damage the Hessians have done to that country during the latter part of their stay there, they have in a manner lived upon free quarters there. It now is necessary to see whether the Land grave will pay the damages to which he has been condemned or whether he must be forced to do it.
Having nothing in particular to add I will not trespass longer upon your Majesty's leisure...

I hope your Majesty will excuse the freedom I take in writing to you so very soon again after my last letter I had the honour of sending you by the quarterly messenger; but as the time is now arrived, when, by the presence of the whole Regiment, I am enabled to learn the practise of those duties attending my present station in the military line, of which I have hitherto been most attentively occupied to learn the theory, I thought it my duty to write to your Majesty a short account of my present occupations. Every morning between eight & nine I go out with the Regiment to exercise, and I pay the most exact attention to the private exercise of each Company by itself, that when the whole comes to join into one body I may not be ignorant of my own duty. I have obeyed your Majesty's commands in consulting frequently the opinion of General Freytag, who is so kind as to honour me with his advice upon all occasions, and when in the field I always am guided by the counsel of the Lieutenant. Colonel de Borch; to whose kind attention and indefatigable care I shall ever be infinitely obliged for whatever knowledge I may hereafter gain in my profession.

Every evening is devoted to exercising our body of recruits, at which I am also constantly present. This seemed to meet with the approbation of General Freytag, who has been so kind as to express his satisfaction to me upon that subject. Your Majesty may depend that I shall not omit being present during the whole course of our exercising, at every, even the most trivial, duties of my station, and I shall ever apply myself with the most unremitted attention to everything by which I may attain some perfection in my profession, and be able hereafter when called upon to distinguish myself to the satisfaction of your Majesty, the approbation of my superiors & my own honour: how far I have hitherto applied myself, I humbly appeal to the testimony of my superiors, and for the future I dare flatter myself you will believe me when I say that on the side of goodwill & application I will most certainly not fail.

Without venturing or even wishing to press your Majesty upon the subject of my late request, in regard to being present at the future Spring camp, I shall most humbly wait for your gracious orders in regard to it...

I do myself the honour of writing to your Majesty & begin by informing you that we are well & that our studies are begun all as usual, the Professors who were absent being come back except Professor Phedre who is a little indisposed. The University lost near two hundred students this half year & it has got already a hundred & sixty new students, 60 of which are French, with whom I have not yet had the pleasure of make their acquaintance; one of them is the Prince of Luxemburg. We heard, Sir, the other day Mr. Buhle make his speech upon his admittance to the dignity of Professor, which was reckoned to be very fine. I mention here a person, Sir, whose father your Majesty has seen often walking on the Terrace, the third son of Sir Alexander Crawford who has got a very good character.

According to what I have the honour of mentioning to your Majesty in my last, I on the 11th of June sailed from Port Royal in company with the Amphion, Captain Brown. We had an uncommonly fine passage up to the Havanah, where, as far as is to be seen from the sea, the Spaniards are carrying on vast works. On the 18th we took our departure from the Pan of Metanzas, and having on the 21st got clear through the Gulf of Florida I parted company from the Amphion and proceeded in my way to America, and on the 27th arrived at Halifax, having run above nine hundred leagues in fifteen days, two out of which we lay to, having mistaken the land of Cuba. This uncommon passage was made without a gale of wind, the water was smooth as in a river. Upon my arrival I found Commodore Sawyer ready with his squadron to proceed to Quebec, and he gave me orders to fit as fast as possible, and I hope to be ready in a few days.

I have now to enter on a subject that gives me pain to communicate to your Majesty, which is, Fidge my Surgeon, from length of service and old age, has been obliged to quit the ship, and will deliver this letter to Lord Howe. I take the liberty of strongly recommending him to your Majesty as having been a faithful and diligent servant. He first went to sea in the Venus with the Duke of Cumberland and has ever since been constantly employed. He has been about fifteen months with me and his conduct in the duty of the ship has been most exemplary, and towards myself as an individual during my being out of order he has ever been diligent so as really to merit my esteem. I therefore take the liberty of again recommending him to your Majesty's notice, and have to request your Majesty would be graciously pleased to have him appointed Surgeon to the first Yard that falls vacant: if I may so far presume as to mention that Fidge is from the town of Portsmouth, and that should that Yard fall vacant, your Majesty would confer an additional favour on him by promoting him to that place.

My stay at Halifax is so short, and I have really had so much duty to get the ship ready for sea and to take my share of the port duty that I have scarce been able to take a pen in hand. Nothing has occurred since I arrived. Tomorrow
Commodore Sawyer sails with the fleet for Quebec, the Lender, Ariadne, Resource, Pegasus and Weasel brigg; the Brisk sloop of war is gone up the Bay of Fundy. I shall do myself the honour of writing to your Majesty all our transactions up the river St. Laurence.

note.value: 386 THE KING TO THE DUKE OF GLOUCESTER

text.p: My dear brother, your letter of the 22d of June which was delivered to me by Mr Vincent is a proof that you are convinced of my real affection for you, and as such, that I must be thoroughly interested in whatever concerns you, and particularly in the welfare of your children. From these motives I have taken every possible means without running the risk of your being refused, to enquire for a gentlewoman who you may safely place about your daughter, and have at last by the channel of Lord Harcourt found one that I flatter myself will fully answer your expectations. She is Miss Dee, the sister of the widow of Commodore Johston. By the report I have received she is above forty, mistress of French, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish and English; she used to sing remarkably well for a gentlewoman and plays admirably on the harpsichord; having strict religious principles but unattended with bigotry, and is very cheerful. Mr Vincent has at my desire seen her and is therefore enabled to answer any questions on which you very naturally may wish to be informed. Such an addition to your family must be an increase of expense as also your well-advised idea of sending your son to an University; I therefore intend granting to you an Irish pension that these may be defrayed without inconvenience to you. Indeed, my brother, I shall ever be happy to convince you of my real sentiments of affection.

I cannot conclude without assuring you of the joy I feel at the return of my second son who, I flatter myself, will prove a real comfort to me. The good character he has acquired whilst abroad will, I trust, stimulate him to avoid hurting it in this dangerous and dissipated country.

After the strong & repeated assurances you gave me in writing on my relieving your debts, which were in the most solemn manner renewed when I consented you should receive the pay of Colonel of my Electoral Regiment of Foot Guards, that you would never again fall into that disgraceful situation, it is easy to conceive how much I am offended at your having not only continued the same shameful conduct, but by those assurances shown you have wilfully and knowingly added untruth to the former errors. Nay, the pay of Colonel has been employed in futile addition to the Band of Music and Drummers of the Regiment, contrary to the regulations laid down by me in that service, and the other expenses have been incurred by building, altering and changing carriages, besides buying and keeping horses unknown to me and contrary to my express orders. I have allowed you the use of my carriages, and of sufficient horses for your use, to which you have added all those which you must have known when once come to my knowledge would incur my highest disapprobation. From the Prince of Wales I have learnt that you have ordered another carriage from hence, and applied to him to pay for it, which he, very properly knowing it would be disagreeable to me, has declined doing. I have therefore by this messenger sent to the Field Marshal my express orders that every addition of musicians, drummers, or any other article in the Guards you have added to what was the state when Prince Charles of Mecklenburgh resigned the Regiment, be instantly discharged & no innovation of the most trifling kind permitted. I cannot keep up a due subordination unless I make the world see my sons must not presume to alter any regulations I have made. And I have at the same time written to Lieutenant. Colonel Wangenheim that all the carriages you have bought, & the horses, must instantly be sold, and any servants you have engaged, exclusive of Rymer who I send abroad with you, must be discharged. I should have flattered myself that the having placed you in the Army would have opened your ideas & have drawn you from spending your time in a manner so much below you. I fear by this you have no turn to what you pretended to look on as the hight of your wishes. But to try if it be not possible to put some ideas into you more becoming of your birth & station, I will instantly send you on your travels, and have therefore sent a positive and explicit instruction to Lieutenant. Colonel Wangenheim how he is to conduct you. He shall give you a copy of it, and the only chance you can possibly have of regaining my affection or opinion will depend on your most implicitly obeying it. And he will lose my confidence and protection entirely if he omits acquainting me with any the smallest attempt in you, of varying from what I have there laid down. You will find I have been forced even to mention points regarding your dress that I should have thought below my notice, but your absurd singularities made it absolutely requisite to prevent your exposing yourself.

On Thursday I received an account of the death of the Bishop of Hereford, but did not choose to write to Mr. Pitt on the subject till the event should be confirmed; last night arrived a letter from Lord Oxford desiring it to be communicated to me, by which I find his brother dyed of a stoppage and inflammation in the bowels. This vacates a good Bishopric, for which I shall expect from Mr. Pitt an application for some Cambridge head of an House, probably the Master of Jesus. It is a desirable thing to me that the Deanery of Windsor should be in in the hands of a respectable man, and as he is an officer of the Garter, wish at least that his name should be of note. It has occurred to me that by removing the Bishop of Carlisle to the Deanery, which is £1,000 per annum , Mr. Pitt could then recommend to the Residentiary of St. Pal's, which is worth £800; the additional £200 the Bishop will get will just pay for a London house. I write my first thoughts to prevent applications; no one has a guess of my intentions.

note.value: 463 THE DUKE OF YORK TO THE KING

text.p: Your Majesty does me but justice in being convinced how anxiously I wished to be informed of your safe arrival at Cheltenham, and I cannot sufficiently express to you, Sir, how much I feel your goodness in acquainting me with it yourself. By everything that I had heard, the country through which your Majesty was to pass, though rich, is by no means a beautiful part of England, but I am informed that the banks of the Severn are reckoned exceedingly romantic. I have not as yet been able to settle myself at Oatlands, but am busily employed in putting everything to rights there for my inhabiting it as soon as possible. Your Majesty is certainly perfectly right in what you are pleased to mention concerning the kind of carts which it will be most advisable to make use of in order to transport the garden stuff &c. from Oatlands to London, and I shall certainly take care to follow so good an example and advice. It shall certainly ever by my first care to seize every opportunity to pay my respects to your Majesty and to assure you in person, Sir, how much I glory in being ever, Sir,

note.value: 464 LETTERS FROM PRINCE EDWARD TO THE KING

text.p:
Permit me to express my gratitude to your Majesty for the very gracious letter of the 27th of June with which you have honoured me. I have this moment received it, and consider it to be my first duty to endeavour to convince you of those sentiments of my most devoted and grateful acknowledgment, which I know better how to feel than how to express. This gracious letter of your Majesty so anxiously and so earnestly wished for gives me a glimmering of hope, and that expectation which I know your heart will now allow me to form, of once again recovering your favour and making you forget the past, will make me redouble my exertions and attention never to fall into my former errors again, and punctually to obey your commands. Should I perhaps by accident offend you in
trifles, deign to lay to the charge of youthful failure that which never can proceed from want of good will or of the firm resolution never to take a step without being first sure of your approbation.

Your Majesty's goodness in allowing me to drive a phaeton is certainly the most sufficient command for me not to abuse of your favour by ever thinking either of buying carriage, horse or harness as long as it is not your pleasure that I should; and in regard to riding out of the manage, your Majesty may depend that I never shall think of doing it without your full and entire permission to do so. I certainly will also not be guilty of the indiscretion to trouble you any more upon that head, only venture now to express the wish, should the continuation of my conduct be to the satisfaction and contentment of your Majesty, that you would perhaps then be inclined to grant me that indulgence.

Your Majesty's kindness in expressing only a wish of my applying myself to subjects that might improve my understanding, at the moment when you might have laid your commands upon me, convinces me that you are persuaded how truly every wish of yours is a sacred order for me, and I hope that in the very first accounts which your Majesty will receive from Lieutenant. Colonel Wanghenhyme, you will be satisfied with the attention I have immediately paid to your desire.
Before I conclude, permit me to express my joy upon your recovery from your late illness, and I hope your Majesty will not want any assertions to convince you of my sincerity.

note.value: 464 LETTERS FROM PRINCE EDWARD TO THE KING

text.p: The first lines which my hand is able to trace since my recovery from a violent rheumatism attended with fever, which nearly deprived me of the total use of both my hands, my duty as well as my inclination lead me to address to your Majesty. Did I not suppose that you were perfectly informed by Colonel de Wanghenhyme of everything relative to our late Tour into Switzerland, I should have ventured to have troubled your Majesty with a short description of it, but as I fear that being already acquainted with it such an account might only tire your patience, I will confine myself to assuring you, as far as I am a judge of it, it has presented to my view more romantic and extraordinary scenes than I have ever had occasion to see before.

Permit me humbly to inform myself if your Majesty has met with that assistance from the Cheltenham waters, which my sisters and myself have most anxiously joined in wishing you to receive. In the last letter which I received from Princess Royal, I found the most flattering accounts of your total recovery, and nothing is now wanting to my complete satisfaction but the honour of receiving the same happy news from your Majesty's own hand.

Emboldened by you Majesty's goodness to me upon all occasions, I hope it is not too much presumption in me, if I conclude this letter with an humble request to you for some addition to my present pocket allowance. Should you be inclined to gratify this wish of mine, your Majesty may depend that my gratitude will ever be equal, whatever you will judge proper to determine.
Flattering myself with the hopes of being honoured by you with a gracious answer, I subscribe myself, with the deepest respect.

The unexpected manner in which your Majesty thought proper to order the ship I have the honour to command to America, obliged me, though very reluctantly, to express my sentiments on the subject in a more explicit manner than I have ever yet done. In the present situation, from the manner in which I was ordered, it is plain that the step originated solely in the breast of your Majesty, who in this case I am only to regard as my father, and in the course of this letter I shall address myself I hope with the respect due to a father and the duty due to the Sovereign.

Upon the late hostile appearances your Majesty, out of your usual paternal tenderness, thought proper to order me home from a situation in which I was placed at my own desire for the space of three years to gain local professional knowledge. The orders requiring me to proceed abroad in 1786 I executed with willingness and alacrity, being both myself, officers, and men ready to expect
such orders. During the twenty months I was abroad, from the sudden transitions from heat to cold and from cold to heat, together with the very relaxed habit of body I had contracted in the West Indies, I was well aware that a continuance of the first plan would prove detrimental to my health. However, from the consciousness that part of my complaint being venereal and consequently having originated through my own indiscretion, I was determined in November 1787 to have made one more trial of the West Indies, though contrary to the express desire of all physical men I had consulted. In this determination I was when orders unexpectedly were sent for my recall. I refer your Majesty to Admiral Sawyer for the manner in which I received the news. As an officer wishing for a war to distinguish myself it afforded me the greatest satisfaction, but again being apprehensive that every thing might be settled I was sorry to cross the Atlantic Ocean to return abroad again. From the moment I arrived in England, which was December 1787, till my first sailing in last June I uniformly studied to remain at home for two reasons: my health, and the certainty of the points for which I had been originally detached abroad, being fully answered, and for a third very material reason, the knowledge of there being no possibility of learning the manuevres of a fleet of foreign service. From the length of time I have had the honour of serving your Majesty I ought and am confident I am adequate to conduct any ship in the world, and am thoroughly acquainted with all the forms of service. My inexperience of fleets urged me to solicit to be employed with them, where I likewise kept up my acquired knowledge and improved daily, as I have done whilst under the command of Admiral Gower. whether I have gained the Admiral's approbation rests with himself. I can safely say no officer wished more ardently or strove more strenuously for the good of the service than I have uniformly done. I do not deny the idea of remaining in England was another motive for my wishing to serve with the Rear-Admiral. I see no harm in expressing a wish to serve at home: with this desire I uniformly asked to be employed on home service. London, believe me, Sir, is the last place in your Majesty's dominions I wish to visit. I do not deny my partiality for Devonshire: my connections there are such as I am by no means ashamed of, and after having been so long in that part of England I confess I am attached to it. When your Majesty's pleasure was signified to me that I should last April return to my former situation, I then made no complaint and should have sailed the following day had not the guard ships been suddenly ordered out: and upon your Majesty's further directions respecting my destination after the cruise I was equally ready to obey, though very much against my inclination, but after having been three weeks at sea and returning in sight of the Lizard, and then to find unexpected orders to proceed abroad without anchoring, is I must confess in time of peace very hard. Had it been intimated to me that it was to be the case, then indeed every body would have been prepared. With respect to myself I cannot help feeling it, but the
situation of the officers and men under my command is very different from their having been naturally led to suppose some little time would have been given after our cruise to prepare themselves for a foreign voyage. The men are in a peculiar hard situation, for from the moment your Majesty honoured me with the command of a ship I have endeavoured to form the men as much as possible from the country round Plymouth, and the most part of them are married, and have left their wives and families unprovided for, having made no provision for them during our absence. I cannot help mentioning the satisfaction I received from the conduct of the officers and men on this occasion.

Having expatiated on this matter, I shall now no longer detain your Majesty but to make one remark more, which is, that I trust the manner in which this letter is wrote will appear to your Majesty to be by no means dictated by passion, heat, or disappointment, but to be the result of my thoughts when cool, sedate, and temperate, and likewise that the language is conformable to the respect due from a son to his parent.
Before I conclude, I must add that my constant endeavours shall be ever exerted to prove by my future conduct both in my public and private situation of life that I am

According to your particular desire I send you here an account of the books I make use of. With Mr Less I make use of the Holy Bible and read on Saturdays a book written by Dr Sack, a Compilation of the Answers the Hereditary Prince of Prussia made at the ceremony of his Confirmation.

Mr. Tatter makes use of a book well known by you, I suppose: Putter's Entwickelung der Teutschen Staatsverfassung, in order the better to explain what Putter has wrote in his extract. In mathematics I make use of Schultz's Logarithmitical Tables, Mr Lichtenberg thinking them preferable to Sherwin's. Frequent recourse is likewise made to Kastner's book of mathematics. When alone I read in German Smith's History of Germany, a very well wrote book. That I may not forget my English, which I am sorry to say I speak very incorrectly now, I read the Spectator, Guardian, Goldsmith, and Hume's History of England. I have just finished Sallust in Latin, but know not yet what book I am now to read, as Professors Heyne and Buhle are at this instant absent from Gottingen, but as soon as I know I will immediately inform you. This morning has Mr Putter finished his Lecture on the German history, having brought the history down to the last treaty between England & Prussia.

I am very happy to be able to tell you that Augustus passed a very good night
& finds himself so much better today as to have been able to set up half an hour this morning. I hope with all my heart that he may continue to recover daily & be soon again a stout man.

When I wrote the rough draught of my letter to Colonel Malortie on Thursday evening the 16th I intended to write also to you, but in that night had one of the spasms in my stomach which, with the consequences of removing it, left me too weak to write till this day. I shall go to St. James's to show I am not so ill as some have thought, but shall certainly have for the rest of my life a flannel clothing next to my skin.

As Dr. Zimmerman thinks you should after so many attacks avoid a cold Winter, I sent my rough draft that no time might be lost in preparing for your going to a mild climate for this Winter. I am grieved to part you from your brothers and to interrupt your studies, but the first object I want you to acquire is health. I am certain your own good sense will make you grasp at every advancement of information you can obtain not detrimental to your health, and keep your various studies at Gottingen so much in practice that on returning there you may not be found to have lost ground; to have advanced is impossible. I cannot add more than the having received your last letter, which gave me great pleasure, as it shows a sensibility of heart and gratitude to Malortie and the rest of the gentlemen for their attentions during your illness.

It would be very different to the feelings of my heart if I omitted the first post I take up my pen writing to you, as it is impossible for a son to have shown more filial affection than has appeared in your letters during my long and severe illness; but what has given me the greatest comfort is that it was accompanied with that thorough reliance on the goodness as well as wisdom of our Great Creator, on whom alone we can rely for support in the hour of affliction or for guidance in that of prosperity. By the mercy of the Almighty, I am not only free from any complaint but truly in perfect health. At the same time I shall carefully avoid every kind of bustle or fatigue, that I may thoroughly acquire my former vigour of body; that of mind I cannot wish to be more completely reinstated than at this hour. May Heaven continue to so direct your steps that you may daily become more deserving of the affection of your parents, relations, and of all good men, and that you may never forget that the House of Hanover have ever been famous for their integrity and for true courage when the dictates of justice not of lucre called them forth as assertors of the rights of the Germanic Constitution.

Permit me to have the honour of addressing these lines to your Majesty to return you my most humble and devoted thanks for your graciously naming me to the command of the English Fuzileers, of which I was yesterday informed by a letter from Sir George Young, addressed to me in consequence of your orders.

I am too sensible of the weakness of my own health to think that I should ever be able sufficiently to acknowledge so gracious a mark of your Majesty's kindness; but though my faculties be weak, my endeavours to render myself not undeserving of your Majesty's favour shall be the more strenuous, and, if through levity or want of thought I may not perhaps always have acted up to your wishes, I hope you are convinced too well of my attachment to your person ever to think me capable of offending you intentionally. I must therefore consider this fresh mark of your goodness as a convincing proof that though I perhaps have often had the misfortune to meet with your displeasure, you are nevertheless always so gracious as to forget and to forgive.

So much, Sir, for the feeble expressions of my gratitude. I have now one
object more concerning which I hope it may not be too much presumption to hope that your Majesty will deign to favour me with a gracious answer. As your Majesty has conferred so very great a favour upon me in appointing me to the command of a Regiment in the British service, deign only to add that of consenting to my joining my corps. At the same time that I humbly request your permission upon this subject, you may be convinced that, as long as it is not your wish or your order that I should have the honour of waiting upon you in London, I shall not even express a desire that might be contrary to your intention, and if you deign to consent to my present request, permit me to assure you that I shall never ask permission to quit the quarters or garrison of my Regiment till you shall honour me with express orders to that purpose, hoping that should it be ordered on foreign service you will not object to my following it to the place of its destination.

Before I conclude, permit me to mention to your Majesty that I cannot forget the generous manner in which my brother Frederic declined the command of the Hannoverian Guards when offered to him by you, before you honoured me with that post. The same motive must at this moment dictate a similar action to me, though I cannot have the same merit, as my action is but the copy of his. In case, therefore, that it should be your Majesty's intention perhaps to place any of my younger brothers at some future period in your Electoral service, I should always regret if I were to stand in their way, by continuing in that post with which I have hitherto been honoured. Permit me, therefore, with the most dutiful submission to your commands to lay at your Majesty's feet the Regiment of Hannoverian Guards, waiting for your further orders whether I am any longer to consider myself as their Colonel.

note.value: 517 THE DUKE OF YORK TO THE KING

text.p: I should not now have ventured to trespass upon your Majesty's leisure or have troubled you upon the subject of my own private affairs, if I did not think it what I owe both to myself and to my brother William, at this instant that his Establishment is to be settled, to lay before your Majesty the real state of our situation. The allowance, Sir, which you have made for us from your Civil List, though more liberal than we could have expected on account of the number of our brothers who certainly have an equal right to share your Majesty's favour with us, yet is by no means adequate to the necessary expenses which our situation in life obliges us to incur. As for myself, having had the good fortune through your Majesty's paternal care of my revenues in Germany, to find a large sum of money saved, I have as yet been able to keep myself out of debt. But having already experienced the unavoidable expenses which belong to my situation, I think it equally a duty I owe to your Majesty and myself respectfully to apprise you, Sir, that I find it utterly impossible to avoid the chance of involving myself in a situation the most repugnant to my own feelings as well as to your Majesty's wishes, I mean that of contracting debts. Upon a former occasion your Majesty was pleased to admit in a great degree the inadequacy of my income, and was graciously pleased to say that although no addition could be afforded from the Civil List, yet that should Parliament think fit to grant a further allowance the proposition should meet with your Majesty's royal approbation. Under the present circumstances, however, I cannot think of applying to anyone but your Majesty, persuaded, that should the idea still continue to meet with your royal concurrence the proper steps will be taken under your Majesty's authority.

note.value: 518 THE DUKE OF CLARENCE TO THE KING

text.p: I embrace this occasion of returning your Majesty my thanks for the allowance your Majesty has been pleased to make for my Establishment. The allowance coming entirely from your Majesty's Civil List I cannot but esteem as extremely liberal on the part of your Majesty, and being well acquainted with your Majesty's sentiments respecting the impropriety and ill consequences of ever being involved in debt, I should esteem myself fortunate to make your Majesty a solemn promise on this subject, but as I trust I shall never fail in the punctual performance of any promise which I make, I think it my duty not to incur the risk of deceiving your Majesty by giving expectations that I can live within the present income and at the same time maintain the character and mode of living inseparable from the relation I bear to your Majesty and my situation in the country.

I beg leave however to repeat my gratitude to your Majesty, being convinced
that your Majesty's kindness and affection which it will ever be my first object to merit would not suffer my income to be inadequate, if the state of your Majesty's Civil List would have allowed of an increase.

What a pleasure is it for me to write to your Majesty on this day so much wished for and which we were so near loosing. Indeed, Sir, I may say that the unhappy accident which deprived your Majesty so long from us has augmented, if any thing can more, our attachement to you. We have felt what it is to loose our King and father, but our Lord listened to the prayers of the distressed widow and her unhappy children & that the same God may guard and comfort your Majesty from all dangers and in all misfortunes is the wish and hope of your Majesty's most dutiful son.

The 25th of last month we had a Ball in a wood for to celebrate your Majesty's recovery. Perhaps it was not so elegant as those that were in London, but I am sure that the joy in everyone's heart was full as warm. During the dinner I went round to see the tables, one of which particularly caught my eye; a description of it may perhaps not be disagreeable to your Majesty. All the oldest peasants were there. I spoke to the oldest of them. He told me that he was 91 and had served George the 1st as Dragoon in the Horse Guards, and that old as he was no one loved the King more than he did. His speech so pleased me that I immediately shook hands with him and drank with all the old fellows your Majesty's health.

Since a fortnight have I been obliged to break off with my studies in military matters, for Hogreve is obliged to be at Hanover during the camp. Hazard had very luckily contrived so that we had just entirely finished with our artillery, and during his absence have we got all the artillery and so far as we are come in fortifications to repeat, I have already drawn a cannon which for the first time Hogrewe tells me is pretty good. The Hessians have likewise a camp the beginning of next month where all their troops will come together, and it just happens so that the feriae are about that time, so that nothing will be lost, for otherwise I do not believe that the Colleges would be very much frequented. We have begun the doctrine of electricity with Lichtenberg. He has been explaining today the deference of positive and negative electricity, of all the course of natural philosophy, electricity is to me the most interesting. The rebellious spirit seems to increase amazingly; we have it now in our neighbourhood. In Cassel have the soldiers rebelled and went to Weissenstein where the Landgrave lives, and threatened if he would not return them their bread which he had taken away, they would burn his Palace; he pacified them then, but the whole matter is not yet decided. The French who are here wear the national cockade, white, blue and red, but it seems that how small soever a number of countrymen may be yet they cannot all be of one party, so there are here six French, out of which there are only two who wear it, and the other four refuse to do it .

note.value: 562 THE KING TO THE LORD CHANCELLOR (LORD THURLOW)

text.p:
It is impossible for me not be be much impressed by whatever you suggest, particularly on legal points. I have therefore fully considered your idea of having a question stated to the Attorney and Solicitor-General whether the intended pension for Lord Auckland can be legally granted. As the measure was proposed by Mr. Pitt I thought it right to communicate your doubt to him, and my idea of refferring it rather to Lord Kenyon, whose legal knowledge is certainly equal and his situation superior to that of the above-mentioned gentlemen; besides he can be applied to in a less public manner. Mr. Pitt felt the propriety of my proposal and assured me he would cordially submit to whatever was the decision of so respectable a person. Having advanced thus far it is now necessary for me to state this proposal to you, who, I am certain, cannot but approve of a reference to Lord Kenyon. For the greater precision I have preferred stating this on paper to a conversation, and shall take no farther step till I hear from you. I also mentioned to Mr. Pitt the industry with which a coolness between you and him is
propagated, and how detrimental such an opinion must be to my affairs; he has in the strongest and most explicit terms assured me of his inclination to live on the most cordial terms with you, and for that purpose is desirous of having a thorough explanation with you on all subjects, and more particularly of those that may have occasioned any shyness. I think I am certain your attachment and I may say affection for me will, when apprised how essential I look on a good understanding between you is to the ease of my mind as well as to the prosperity of public affairs, make you equally desirous of having such intercourse as may effect what I have so much at heart.

At present all our lectures have begun again. I have now from the morning on till noon continually lessons, so that the afternoon I have for my own work. Major Hogrewe is returned from his tour to Osnabruck; he has begun geometry with us, that is to say, so much as is necessary for us to know in order to survey. This we do one day, and the other we repeat the tactics with him. Mr. Less has just finished the course in religion; he intends to repeat some few chapters and then end, for during the 4 years we have gone through the course four times. I continually work for Martens; he now reads a book through with us which he has lately published, it is a Collection of Treaties, which are compiled in the same manner as Wink compiled his. We have to about an hour ago had a great loss for the University in the death of Professor Brands , who, though a young man, yet was endowed with great talents. He died this afternoon at 4 o'clock of a putrid fever. It is at this instant a greater loss for the University as that part of the law has now no Professor who can read it, for Hofrath Claproth, who used to read has been by the physicians forbid to read this summer...

The garrison is now very busy exercising; as often as my hours will permit me I go . The 18th there is the Review of the 1st Regt. of Stockhausen at Mundane. I am invited there to see a new manoeuvre that the old General has invented. The Review is to be on the very spot where in the last War he drove the French away. Lichtenberg has today begun to read again for the first time after an illness of 7 months, where his death was daily expected, I think he will now be quite cured.

After the recovery of my health it has always been my wish and desire, with your Majesty's pleasure, to embrace the profession destined for me already from my tender years, and which was always my darling thought, a thought, I may say I ever nourished from my youth, and imbibed with my daily nourishment. Thank God, Sir, I am now perfectly recovered; my late indisposition was only the measles, and from them I am also perfectly reestablished. In all my desires and wants, my duty and wish prompts me to have recourse to your Majesty's goodness. The fine and noble description of the British Fleets which are preparing, have roused in me a double desire to go with them, a desire that haunts me day and night. During the whole day I do nothing but think of them, and at night but dream of them. The blood of a British subject boils within me, and I wish to be a witness at what is going forwards. The family of Brunswick have always been renowned for their courage; I wish also to show mine, but in a manner the most useful for my country, wherefore, with your Majesty's gracious permission, I would wish to become midshipman. I say only with your Majesty's pleasure, for let my desire be ever so warm, should it interfere with your Majesty's plans I shall give it up immediately, and, cost me what it will, shall endeavour to forget it entirely. However, should there be a possibility I humbly entreat your Majesty. It is no whim, Sir, for the moment. It is a desire I have cultivated from my tender years, and which once your Majesty saw with pleasure. I gave it up once, thinking my week state of health would not admit of it. Now, thank God, I am recovered, the desire comes again, and with your Majesty's gracious pleasure I shall go aboard a ship, the sooner the better. I have consulted my physicians on the occasion. Professor Stromeyer, first Physician, assures me it would be of great use to my health. Professor Fisher's answer was that persons labouring under breast complaints had frequently been entirely cured by the sea air, and that the trial might be made. I have now laid my petition before your Majesty. Does it meet with your Majesty's gracious pleasure, so much the better for me; if not I shall however ever remain

My principal business consists now in reading the different histories of the 7 Years War; in the view of gaining an accurate knowledge of the different places in Silesia I have made myself an extract out of that description made by Archenholtz who served in the late 7 Years War in the Regiment of Forced. I now read the history of it written by the late King. I have just been busy with Major Hograve in learning what is necessary for an officer when in war how one must reconnoitre a country, the necessary precautions that must be taken to place a camp &c., and now we are going to examine carefully some of the chief battles fought in the 7 Years War, as the Battle of Minden according to the plans published of it.

As Hograve served the whole 7 Years War he is able to inform me likewise of such things as are perhaps wanting in the plans. I have just been reading the Memoirs of Count St Germain which General d'Estorff had the goodness to lend to me. It shows very evidently what a continual discord reigned in the French Army during the last war, and proves how prejudicial it is for a country when its commanding Generals sacrifice for their private enmities the good of their country.

My cousin Augustus of Brunswic paid me a visit last week; he is I believe the happiest being in the whole Electorate since he has got a Company; he does talk of nothing but his Company. In my idea it seems to be very agreeable to command a Company, but I cannot say I should think myself content in being able to command a Company; all my aim and my desire is to command once an army and have once the character of being as good a General as the present Duke of Brunswic.

note.value: 616 THE DUKE OF CLARENCE TO THE KING

text.p:
I have thus long deferred having the honour of addressing your Majesty, as the situation hitherto of the Valiant has not afforded matter worthy of your Majesty's perusal. It would be ridiculous in me to give an account of the Fleet as your Majesty must receive the most authentic particulars from the Commander-in-Chief: indeed the Valiant has hitherto so entirely occupied my time that I could not. I am at present satisfied, and, feeling prepared, wait
anxiously for the arrival of Lord Howe. Admiral Barrington ordered the Fleet to exercise without regard to form, but to perfect the men with the guns and sails. He has now reported us fit for service. On board the Valiant I kept everybody employed from five in the morning till nine at night. I should have been remarkably well answered if I had not received a draft from the Scipio of six and thirty men more properly to be called wretches; excepting the gunners and quartermasters I have not a man in the ship either as old as myself or has been as long at sea.
