Another extraordinary circumstance is that none of the seamen have yet had the honour of serving your Majesty: the landsmen are composed of volunteers I raised at Richmond, Roehampton, and in Cornwall. Certainly I cannot say too much of the attention of the officers, but if the men had not of themselves been well inclined, no discipline in this short time could have effected the good order we are now in. At present they are very healthy; they have been very sickly, but by smoking their health is reestablished and I only lost one man. As I expect three and thirty more from the North, upon their arrival I shall weed and then be very well manned indeed. It is a very great satisfaction to see through the whole Fleet the good humour and happiness of the men. I trust, should your Majesty think a war should be declared, that the Fleet will prove their attachment and fidelity and that among the number the Valiant will do her duty: she is a charming ship and I am more and more pleased with her and every body on board of her. I am afraid I have trespassed too much on your Majesty's time.

I refrain saying any thing of your Majesty's health as by all accounts I hear of your Majesty's perfect enjoyment of spirits, which is the strongest indication of what I, together with all my fellow subjects, so ardently wish.

Your letter of the 23d of last month arrived on Wednesday, which has greatly relieved the Queen and your sisters as well as me from our anxieties on the return of your complaints, as we trust that now the crisis of the disorder is over and that every subsequent accounts will prove you are recovering. I should not do justice to what ought ever to be uppermost in our thoughts did I did express that thanks to the All-Wise Ruler of the Universe for his having
supported you on this occasion, and my joy that you are so well grounded in those principles of religion which alone can enable us to support either prosperity or adversity. The attention of those who surround you must have given pleasure, and the medical gentlemen seem to have shown great skill and now are fully acquainted with the nature of your complaint, and therefore will, I trust, be the better able to keep off returns of it. I shall not add more but that I ever remain

I could not suffer General O'Hara to leave us without embracing so favourable an opportunity of writing to your Majesty. At the same time I think myself in duty bound to inform you that ever since I have had the
honour of being under his command, if my conduct has merited your approbation, I am indebted for this to his attention & his advice upon every occasion in which my own inexperience might have been the cause of my acting improperly. I hope your Majesty will not consider it as presumption in me, when I mention that I believe hardly ever any Officer who has done his duty with such zeal and activity as General O'Harra has done his, could be more universally and generally regretted on his departure than he will be.

Lieutenant Colonel Symes has requested me to inform your Majesty in the most dutiful and respectful manner that some family affairs of the most material consequence to him require unavoidably his presence in Ireland towards the ensuing Spring; though certainly I shall be a most material loser by his not remaining with me, I am not selfish enough to wish to detain him when his affairs would suffer so considerably as they are likely to do by his absence. However, if your Majesty graciously indulges me with the removal of my Regiment in the Spring to Canada, he has promised, at my particular request, if it meets with your approbation and he can possibly arrange his affairs by that time, to return to me there in the Fall. The very great assistance he has given me, and the very marked liberality of principles which have guided all his actions to me, merit more grateful acknowledgments from me than I can find words to express. I hope your Majesty will not forget his services, and I beg of you to consider that any mark of your approbation conferred on him, I shall consider as very flattering to me.

If you should, in consequence of Colonel Symes's absence, judge it necessary to appoint any other officer to attend me in his room, I venture to submit to your consideration two officers who, to the best of my knowledge, are both respected and esteemed by all who know them. The one has the honour of being one of your Majesty's attendants, Colonel Greville, your Equerry, the other is Major Villettes of the 12th Regt. of Light Dragoons now Aid de Camp to General Pitt. Should you be pleased to approve of one of these two officers, it would be very flattering to me. Before I conclude, may I presume to recommend to your Majesty's favour and protection, when a proper occasion may present itself, Capt. Green, who was so many years in my family? I should not venture to do this, if I did not know him to be equally respectable as a man & as an officer.

note.value: THE KING'S REPLY, QUEEN'S HOUSE, 8 MARCH.

text.p: I have received very regularly letters from you and am most thankful to the Almighty that the mild climate of the south of France seems so thoroughly to agree with you, and I trust that the passing the succeeding winter in the same fine climate with spending the summer months in some mild air will completely restore your health. I am happy you are able to resume part of your studies, which employment will make you with more pleasure enjoy those of relaxation; there is no greater wisdom than so to oeconomise amusements that they shall continue such during life, which, if too much sought after, naturally must sooner or later become irksome; besides, if the mind be not constantly in the habit of serious employment it will lose its energy, and those powers a man may have been blessed with will entirely vanish.

The time of my departure for America is approaching so very near, that though with reluctance, I find myself under the necessity of writing to you on a subject which I wish ever to avoid troubling you with. It is the first expense I was obliged to incur on my arrival here. Your Majesty knows how perfectly unprovided I was with every individual article that was indispensably necessary for me to keep house. Being obliged therefore to purchase, when I first came here, everything which I wanted, & having no person to employ in this business who was able to prevent my being egregiously imposed upon, that expense which in England might have been amply supplied with twelve hundred pounds, has been rather more than doubled here. With the best inclination, not to trouble your Majesty to defray this, and with the best intention of supplying the whole of it, by what I could save from the yearly income you was pleased to allot me, I have been totally unable to do it, from the very great expense with which the keeping house has been attended, owing to the scarcity of provisions on one side, & the most infamous impositions of the merchants, to which we were forced to submit, on the other.

Circumstanced as I am in consequence of this, may I venture to request that your Majesty will assist me in defraying this first expense, which, if you judge it proper, may be deducted from any allowance you may please to regulate when once you may think proper to establish me. I have now mentioned what I thought it necessary to submit to your judgment, and shall conclude with begging you to be convinced that I trust at no future period shall I have occasion to trouble you again on a subject equally irksome to your Majesty to hear and for me to mention.

The hearing the cold you caught by the sudden change of weather has subsided without any visible detriment to your health is the more satisfactory as it gives the best ground for hopes that the excellence of the climate of Hie`res is restoring your lungs to their state, and that another winter in that beautiful island will perfect the cure. I lost no time in authorizing Baron Alvensleben to acquaint Captain Hanstein that I approve of Vevay as your summer residence, agreeable to your wish and the opinion of Doctor Zimmerman, and consequently expect this will reach you there. I am certain you will be cautious during the summer of not overheating yourself, and that you will not take more exercise than may be conducive to enable you to return to Hie`res in perfect health; whatever can give air and avoid fatigue seems to be the mode that should be addopted.

Your Majesty will be so gracious as to excuse my not having wrote sooner; my intention in so doing was to give you an account of what I had seen on the journey and thus render my letter somewhat more interesting as it else would be. Thursday the eleventh of this month I left Marseilles and went as far as Aix, which seemed to me vastly altered for the worse. It was always a dull town but since the last riots it looks quite deserted. In the great street not a soul to be seen and every face bears fear and sorrow upon it. My next day's tour was as far as Tarascon but as nothing remarkable was to be seen on that road I shall not mention anything about it. The Saturday I reached Nimes by the way of Arles. As this town was so famous in ancient times and is still so now on account of its antiquities, my curiosity was very great to see it. We began by examining the famous obelisk erected on the Market place in honour of Louis the Great. It is of Egyptian granite, sixty one feet high and at the base a diameter of seven feet. A part of an ancient Capitol is another beautiful remains of the Romans. It is half an arch supported by two pillars of the Mixed Order, beautiful beyond description. I could not help reflecting on the difference of the times compared now with the present. When the Romans undertook any such building they constructed it with the intention of making it last for ever as a proof of their grandeur. At present all our undertakings are guided by the idea how to make the most money, consequently those are preferred which are the soonest finished, whereas much time is required for rendering them solid.

From the Capitol we went to the Amphitheatre which is much larger than that of Nimes but not so well preserved. The most interesting for me was what I saw last namely the Elision Fields of Arles so famous in ancient times. This is a very extensive piece of ground entirely covered with sarcophagous's. - There is not one of them shut being all opened either by the curiosity of the inhabitants or some travellers. The most valuable are contained within the walls of the Convent of Minimes. Amongst all the sarcophagous's one is particularly remarkable being very well preserved. It is a pagan one and serves at present for a coffin for a Bishop of Arles. Many people have taken the figures for an Assemblage of the Gods, which it is not. It expresses the life of man from the birth to his death. Having seen Nimes already before, I examined the antiquities there very slightly and set out the following morning for Montpellier. I expected a much finer town as what I found it to be. A place so much frequented by strangers ought to have better accommodations. The great walk is the only thing worth seeing here. As for an account of the Canal I shall defer giving any till when I am come to the end of it. My health is at present pretty good though the weather is very cold here. Forgive me, Sir, for having taken up your Majesty's attention so long.

note.value: 685 THE DUKE OF YORK TO THE KING

text.p: Though I know how much your Majesty dislikes in general compliments upon your birthday, yet I trust that you will not regard in that light my congratulations upon this day, that Heaven may shower down its choicest blessings upon your Majesty's head, and that your Majesty may enjoy every health and happiness for a very long series of years, are my constant and most ardent prayers.

I am returned about three days from the Reviews at Magdeburg, which were wonderfully fine. I think there is no comparison between that inspection and the one here; the troops are infinitely finer in point of men and much more exact in
their evolutions. The Duke of Brunswick's Regiment surpasses all the others. There was likewise at Magdeburg four battalions of Fusileers, as they are called here, or rather of Light Infantry, which are really wonderfully good and remarkably well exercised. They are very small men, know perfectly the Light Infantry exercise, and at the same time can act in line as well as any other battalion. The Cavalry likewise at Magdeburg are very good, and I think are very much improved on their horses. This was the first year that the Duke of Weymar appeared as Inspector and he really seemed to have given himself a great deal of trouble. The Duke of Brunswick was not sufficiently recovered to be at the Camp, and therefore General Knobelsdorf as the senior Officer commanded.

note.value: THE KING'S REPLY, QUEEN'S HOUSE, 1 MAY, 8 A.M.

text.p: The most daring outrage to a regular Government committed by the new Society, who yesterday published its manifesto in several of the newspapers, could only be equalled by some of its leaders standing forth the same day to avow their similar sentiments in the House of Commons; and I cannot see any substantial difference in their being joined in debate by Mr. Fox and his not being a member of that Society, but if men are to be found willing to overturn the Constitution of this country, it is most providential they so early cast off the mask, and I am most happy it has given Mr. Pitt so fair an opportunity of avowing sentiments that must endear him to all lovers of good order and our excellent Constitution. It is also very material that many speakers on the side of Opposition have pledged themselves to co-operate in opposing these Reformers as well as so respectable a list of friends of Government.

I received last night the enclosed paper from the Duke of Gloucester; it is drawn up by the same pen from which intelligence was sent on Saturday from the same channel by Lord Sydney to Mr. Dundas. It deserves the attention of Administration, and it seems highly worthy of enquiry whether any large sum of money has been procured for France from Ireland, and what Irishmen are connected with the French emissaries in this country. I desire Mr. Pitt will in my name give the paper this day to Mr. Dundas, that he may have the matter attended to, and I should think it might easily be traced whether Mons. de Pe`rigord has been secretly at London the last week and whether he returned to Dover, and has publicly returned within these two days.

The war on the Continent appearing now to be sure I cannot help expressing my earnest desire of making a campaign, and thereby enlargen my knowledge in the art of war; I should be very happy if your Majesty would be so gracious and permit my serving as volunteer with the Prussian Army which is just marched. You may be assured I shall not neglect any opportunity wherein I may make some progress, and may perfection myself in my capacity as a good officer who may once be made use of for the defence of his King and country.
I took the liberty before I wrote to your Majesty to ask General de Freytag's advice, and he much approves my desire. If you are so gracious and grant this my request, I beg most humbly you may immediately give your orders for my departure to the Prussian Army, and give General de Freytag me necessary instructions to choose me two officers who may accompany me, for my real desire is to perfection myself and not to have a suite which is merely troublesome. Dearest father, this request comes alone from my desire of gaining more experience and knowledge in a service for which I am so passionately fond. I entreat your Majesty to answer me soon, and at the same time either write straight forward to the King of Prussia, or send me the letter that I may take it with me, in order that no time may be lost.

Your Majesty will no doubt be surprised to find I have had a small return of my old complaint. Indeed it does not pain me a little, the more so as I foresee no alteration for the better unless a total change in my present situation takes place. It hurts me to write this, as I know beforehand it will be unpleasant to your Majesty but I have accustomed myself to be on a confidential footing with you, Sir, and therefore cannot conceal my feelings on this occasion. You yourself would be with reason displeased with me were I to act the hypocrite.

My journey is intended for my health but according to the present situation of things it does me more harm than good. I am unhappy; and that is the cause of my present indisposition. The two gentleman who are with me, though they conceal their illness, are both unwell, nay very seriously indisposed. I have asked my physician his opinion on the subject who assures me the one has a breast complaint, the other an abscess in the lower part of his stomach. To be constantly surrounded with melancholy faces, with people who suffer, whose temper is soured by their sufferings is more than I can support and makes me truly miserable. Their indisposition prevents my enjoying many parties on account of their not being able to accompany me. Whenever I want to go out they constantly make difficulties who is to accompany me and when we are out are so melancholy that we never exchange ten words together. Jonquieres is so unwell that he can scarcely bear the motion of the carriage and is forced often to get out and walk. Your Majesty will easily imagine it is no amusement for me to drive alone step by step. I have always shown them the greatest attention, never going out without having one of them with me because it is your Majesty's pleasure and that I never would act against it. At the same time I cannot but find it hard that they should make any difficulty to my going anywhere when I signify a wish for it and that it is a very harmless thing. Such sort of things hurt me much. I know my situation and the inconveniences attending my rank which I never make any difficulty to submit to, but I think a line may be drawn now, especially as I feel myself of an age to begin to act for myself. My wishes are not unreasonable, Sir. My desire is not to run about the town or any such ideas like these - but to be able to say when I like a society there I will go. Till now my conduct has been approved of and I trust it ever will be so. Your Majesty's wish is an order for me. My whole desire is to act according to your satisfaction. With your Majesty's leave I wish to propose a fixed sum for the expenses of my dress and pocket money, the account of which I will send in to you, Sir. This seems to me a good method to know the value of money. Your Majesty has had my word never to make any debts so that you may faithfully rely upon my contenting myself with whatever you think proper to give me. I will here conclude finding myself too weak to continue.

note.value: 778 THE DUKE OF YORK TO THE KING

text.p: I think it my duty to acquaint your Majesty with a very shocking and unfortunate affair which has happened and which concerns General Guydickens of the 3d Regiment of Foot Guards, whose character till now has ever stood unimpeached in every light, and whose situation both in the Army and in her Majesty's family renders it still more melancholy. Indeed I should have made my report to your Majesty sooner, if I had not waited to be able to give your Majesty every intelligence possible concerning this dreadful affair.

On Friday as soon as I arrived upon the Parade of the 2d Battalion of the Coldstream, a soldier whose name is Cannon brought to me a prisoner whom he had just taken upon the Parade, and whom he said he and a Grenadier of the name of Heywood, had caught the evening before in a very indecent situation with a gentleman in Hyde Park, but who had escaped from him at that time. At the same time Captain Hawgill, the Adjutant in Waiting brought me a report from a Sergeant of the Magazine Guard that Heywood was in confinement there by order of General Guydickens for an assault upon him, and also added that General Guydickens was the person whom the soldiers said they had caught with the other prisoner in the most indecent situation and who after some resistance the Grenadier had carried to the Magazine Guard, but when he had charged the Sergeant with him, the Sergeant, knowing him, would not take charge of him, when the General came forwards and naming himself ordered the Sergeant to confine Heywood and a plasterer who had come up during the scuffle. While Captain Hawgill was making this report to me, a Sergeant of the 3d Regt. brought Heywood to me upon the Parade, and told me that General Guydickens had ordered him to be set at liberty. As this affair however had made so much noise I ordered these different people to be kept separate till after the Parade, and then examined them myself separately, and am sorry to say that I found their different accounts agree perfectly. The only thing therefore that I thought I had to do was to send Captain Hawgill immediately to General Guydickens to acquaint him with what had passed, and to tell him that if he felt himself innocent, it was incumbent upon him to clear his character fully, but if not that the only thing he had to do was to send in his resignation and to fly the country immediately and that in consequence of his unfortunate circumstances and of his former good character that I would apply to your Majesty for leave for him to sell his Company. The General appeared exceedingly shocked, and protested his innocence, but seemed to be so distressed that he did not know what to do. It was not till late on Friday evening that the different evidences were examined before the Justices in Bow Street, and they were again examined Saturday and yesterday, and I am sorry to add that these evidences appeared so clear and connected, that the prisoner was fully committed
to take his trial, and General Guydickens has given bail this morning to stand his trial likewise. It is much to be hoped that the poor man is innocent, though unfortunately appearances are strongly against him. I trust however that as this unfortunate case must come to a public trial your Majesty will be graciously pleased to suspend your judgement till that is over. The Regiment has behaved most exceedingly well upon it and have resolved to give the General every assistance in their power to clear himself from this shocking accusation.

I am afraid I have already trespassed too long upon your Majesty's leisure, but I thought it my duty to lay the whole affair before Your Majesty on account of the General's situation both as an officer and having the honour to belong to the Queen's family at the same time that I hope that your Majesty will not disapprove of what I have had to do in this very unfortunate affair.

I embrace the very first opportunity which has offered since my return from Upper Canada, to inform your Majesty that after being
absent only twenty six days, I arrived here on the 6th of the month, having visited every post occupied by any even the smallest detachment of your troops throughout all Canada, except Michillimakinac, Detroit, and Oswego. This latter place I was prevented from seeing by a violent storm which overtook us in our passage across Lake Ontario, and thus rendered it a matter of utter impossibility for me to reach the fort. I had the satisfaction during my tour of seeing every regiment, except the 24th, now in Canada, having met the Queen's Rangers, and the 5th Regiment at Niagara, and being appointed by Major-General Clarke Reviewing Officer for the Regiments in Lower Canada, in which capacity I saw the 26th, and the first and second Battalions of the 60th.

A very large deputation from the Indians of all the neighbouring nations came to Niagara to wait my arrival, as soon as they heard that I was to visit Upper Canada. Their professions of attachment to your Majesty and the British Government were extremely warm, and they would not on any account return home to their tribes till they had made me faithfully promise that in the name of them all I should inform you, in the strongest terms I could find, of their zealous attachment to your person, and of their utmost readiness at all times to obey any commands with which you may at any time choose to honour them. I hope you will pardon my presumption in troubling you with this short recital, but I was anxious for your Majesty to see how I had employed the time of my absence.

May I presume now, Sir, to request your permission for me to visit the American States in the winter at the close of 1793 or commencement of 1794, in case it should be your Majesty's intention that I should be at that period in this part of the world. Two months, or ten weeks at the utmost, would enable me to visit any part which it is an object for me to see, either in a military point of view, or as a traveller, according to the best information which I have been able to obtain. Should my request not meet with your Majesty's approbation, I must humbly entreat you to overlook my indiscretion in making it. My anxiety never to omit any of the duties of my profession has made me request your indulgence at a season when the severity of the climate prevents any military pursuit from being attended to, except the common routine of interior economy and daily duty. May I presume to hope that the Queen will, through you, Sir, accept of the assurances of my most devoted attachment, and my sisters of those of my most affectionate love.

Your Majesty has made me inexpressibly happy by your graciousness towards me. I return you my most humble thancks, and I assure you, Sir, I will pay such attention to my duty and to my behaviour as shall deserve your approbation, this being the only means of proving to you my gratitude for your goodness to me. I hope to begin soon to learn the service, and General Freytag has promised he would give his orders for it. I will apply myself as much as I can to render myself capable of fulfilling the post your Majesty has given me. You have rendered me doubly happy in placing me a` la suite of the Guards a Redgment to which I always have wished to belong and which certainly is one of the best in your service. Particularly at this present moment am I glad to be in it, I mean, if your Dominions should be attacked by the French, for then I should perhaps have an opportunity of showing you the ardour I have of fighting for my King and country, which shall always be the desire of him who is for ever

Though I had the honour of writing to your Majesty last post, yet as this town has been unquiet again, and that the circumstances are in general exaggerated when at so great a distance, I have taken up my pen in order to give you, Sir, as correct a detail as possible.

Ever since the last disturbance that took place in January, the people have been far from being satisfied. Every moment false alarms have been given, letters pretended to have been found encouraging uproars, and every night, one was informed, was to be a new scene of confusion. Last Sunday the common people, who are vastly well informed of everything that is going on here, as Government takes its spies from that class, found out that the Neapolitan Minister had bought to a very large amount of corn not only for the the consumption of Naples but likewise in part for the French. This certainly displeased them, and what added to the discontent was that the Neapolitan Minister had not strictly kept to the agreement he had made. In consequence of this a mob assembled tumultuously about his house, and had not the military force been called in, which is much respected here, he might have fared badly.

On the Monday following, a Frenchman belonging to the French Hospital happened to have a dispute with a servant of the Secretary of State. In the heat of the quarrel he drew a knife, and, showing it the footman, swore it should be made use of to dispatch him, his master, and the Pope. Some persons hearing the conversation pursued the man, who found means to escape and conceal himself in the Hospital. It was a good while before he could be found, which gave time to the people to assemble, and their number amounted to about five thousand. They wanted to set fire to the Hospital and burn all the French that were in it, but were prevented by the soldiers, who had great difficulty to convey the criminal to prison, the crowd being so exasperated that they wished to kill him. In the course of the two ensuing nights they visited all the houses inhabited by French and burnt even the furniture of one of them. No lives were lost though. The Pope has had some of the heads of these disturbances put in prison, which it is hoped will quiet everything. He has published a very severe Decree to prevent all strangers from being insulted, and now everything is going on as it ought. Some English were rather ill treated here, but everything has been made up amicably and Government has shown itself particularly attentive to them.

note.value: THE KING TO THE DUKE OF YORK
FROM THE KING, QUEEN'S HOUSE, 7 MARCH.

text.p: Last night I received your letters of the 28th of the last and 2d of the present month. They gave me thorough satisfaction both as to your manner of conducting yourself at The Hague and as to your opinion of the present situation of things there; but I trust by Lord Auckland's dispatch of the 4th that your arrival has proved of the greatest utility by effecting a more decisive mode of conducting business and more activity in the performance of the orders given.

Every step is taking here to add to the aquatic preparations making in Holland for the defence of the Meuse, the good effect of which will soon be found if the present east wind does not prevent the vessels from sailing that are ordered for that service.

Major-General Abercrombie has orders to proceed from Scotland with the 37th and 53d Regiments of Foot as a farther reinforcement, and probably the 14th Regiment of Foot from Dover will arrive previously. Lieutenant. Colonel Moncrieff, whose experience in America will render him an useful adviser not only for the defence of the Meuse, but also as to other operations, will embark with this Regiment.

You may depend on my sending Colonel Sporken in a few days, but it is thought material he should stay here till the answer arrives from Hanover how soon the first four thousand men can begin their march towards Holland, and as by your letters the Prince of Orange has not yet fixed where they shall enter the Republic, nor what quarters shall be prepared for them, this delay cannot be of much consequence.
My accounts from Oatlands are very favourable and I trust I shall see the Duchess on Monday at Windsor.

I hope that your Majesty will pardon my presumption in troubling you with these lines at a moment when I am sensible that your time must be taken up with attention to matters of the highest importance; I confess,
indeed, that I trust the subject on which I am going to address you will plead my excuse. With these expectations, allow me, Sir, to proceed.

The present situation of affairs in Europe is so awful, that I cannot help feeling the greatest anxiety when I reflect at what a distance I am at this period from your person, and I cannot refrain from expressing a most earnest wish to be allowed at this moment to return to England. I hope, Sir, that you are fully persuaded how ready I am to obey with the utmost cheerfulness your commands for my remaining abroad in America or elsewhere for any period or in any manner which you may please to point out. But, at this critical conjuncture I am sure that your Majesty must feel how natural it is for a son, possessed of the most devoted filial attachment to his parents, and for a subject professing the most loyal and dutiful zeal for his Sovereign, to wish that he may be permitted to approach his person, at a time when it becomes the first duty in every one, much more in every branch of his own family, to prove their loyalty and zeal.

Perhaps, Sir, in the line of my profession an opportunity may now offer in which my services may be useful to my Sovereign, and to my country. Permit me then, Sir, if this should be the case, by allowing me to return home, to have an opportunity of personally offering my exertions as far as my abilities extend in any situation in which you may think fit to employ me.

I am confident that every one of your Majesty's children must at this moment vie with each other in endeavouring, by giving daily proofs of their duty and attachment to your person, to make up to you for that load of cares which the present state of public affairs must have brought upon your mind. Allow me then, Sir, to hope that I am not to be the only one who is to be deprived of the blessing of exerting himself in so dear a cause.

I have presumed to write to the Queen also, this day, to request that she will render the humble offer of my services acceptable to you, and obtain your acquiescence to my returning home, that I may have the opportunity of personally proving those sentiments of the most devoted attachment for you, and for her Majesty, which I shall ever be proud to profess.

Since the 30th am I arrived here. The Regiment has been exactly six weeks on its march, and this is the very first opportunity I have had of writing since my departure from Hanover. To my greatest joy was I yesterday for the first time present at a skirmish between the Imperial Chevaux Lagers and the French Sans Culottes; I had the happiness of being present from the very beginning, though our Regiment had not the honour of sharing with the Imperialists. I was riding with the Veldmarschall Freytag reconnoitring when at once we met an Imperial Officer with 24 horses who told me a party of French was coming on, I embraced with the greatest eagerness ye opportunity of sharing in the sport. The first shot that the Hanoverian Grenadier battalion fired had effect and a driver of the piece of cannon which afterwards was taken fell dead on the spot, for as we advanced I saw the corpse; the fellow was shot through the nose. The first battalion of Diepenbrocke was present; our 2 Regiments, rather I should say four squadrons laying about two English miles from Tourney could come up quick enough to share in the glory; but today we are advanced and have taken our quarters at Aines about a half hour on the left of the Imperial camp; the 1st and 4th Regiments of Heavy Cavalry are encamped, but we, having no tents with us, are in cantonments. One cannot conceive more brave fellows than the Austrian Chevaux Lagers, they gave quarter to no one except one poor boy, and this seemed to be disagreeable to them. My most sanguine wishes are that we may have very soon an opportunity of showing that we Light Dragoons can also take cannon. It was very curious that it had been almost the case that we on our arrival here should have seen the enemy, for about half an hour from the town I got orders from the Duke to advance with the 2 Squadrons; this was a piece of news which rendered us very happy, but unluckily these hopes were soon lost by a second order to enter our quarters which were at La Tomb. Frederic was yesterday the whole time as well as the Veldmarschall present at this affair; the cannon which we took is a very neat piece, well appointed; we have also got the munition car.

Since the day I marched from Hanover I have not seen Dolly, but am told he is very well and is vastly pleased with his march. He is at present not yet here but I hope we shall soon get him again here by us. I cannot enough praise the Regiment which I have the honour of commanding. I have not had any reason to find any fault since the very beginning of our march; even I can give you my word of honour that I have not found a single soldier drunk which is saying much when one comes to consider that on the first day's march through Hanover all the
Dragoons' good friends on their taking leave offered them brandy enough, and many Dragoons has spared his money in order to buy some forage for his horse when ours was not arrived; and with such fellows it is a true pleasure to attack the enemy. I shall certainly now take every opportunity of writing to your Majesty as is possible.

note.value: FROM THE CAMP AT ESTREUX, 4 JUNE 1793.

text.p:
I cannot let this messenger go off without wishing your Majesty sincerely joy of this day, and of many many very happy returns of it. This midday I have dined at Frederick's, and I have had the honour and pleasure of drinking your Majesty's health in a very large company, and, I may certainly say, of very loyal subjects. Since I have had the honour of writing to
your Majesty nothing of great consequence has happened: we are still always enclosing Valenciennes. Last Sunday night the first parallel was opened at about 400 yards from the fortress without a single shot being fired at us. Last night 1200 Hannoverians marched with almost the same success: at least not a single one has been wounded. And I am very happy to say that Colonel Moncriefe, the Chief Engineer, is extremely well contented with them. The heavy artillery is not yet arrived and I hear that it will last some days before it will arrive quite here. Last Saturday I have had the inspection of the right wing, as Field Officer of the day. I was employed the greatest part of the night with General Hammerstein in placing the piquetes which were very much advanced, and in the morning at three o. clock I went with him to Briquette, a village where there is a battalion always on duty and which is relieved every night, which is only 800 yards from Valenciennes. I was very happy of doing this duty for by that a very clear idea how our chain of posts is placed. I wish nothing more than that Valenciennes may be soon taken; certainly nobody will be more happy than .

note.value: THE KING'S REPLY, WINDSOR, 14 OCT., 7.50 P.M.

text.p: I have this instant received Mr. Secretary Dundas's letter enclosing the one Mr. Adam has written to him. I own I had flattered myself that with the unpleasant account there would have been some plan for alleviating my son's affairs; indeed, it seems to me that, after the very creditable part he has acted in the present War it is incumbent on every servant of the Crown to join in finding some means of releaving him. I desire therefore Mr. Dundas will show the whole to Mr. Pitt, who I am certain will see the propriety as well as necessity of having this sum made easy to him; indeed Mr. Dundas must feel that Mr. Adams certainly has informed the Duke of York, in whose hands the business has been put, and consequently the very just ground of disgust that must arise at an interference when not accompanied with remedying the evil.

note.value: 986 THE DUKE OF YORK TO THE KING

text.p: I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your Majesty's most gracious letter of the 12, which Colonel Sporken delivered to me this evening.

I most humbly agree with your Majesty in the absolute necessity which there is that a well digested plan for the next campaign should be arranged and settled between the different Allied powers, but particularly between your Majesty and the Emperor, and in the great detriment which the want of such a plan was to the whole of the last campaign. It is to be hoped that when the Emperor arrives he will be equally sensible of this, and I am sure that if he listens in the least to Count Mercy, he will do everything in his power to convince him of the necessity of it.

Your Majesty will see by my letter to Sir James Murray that I have obeyed your Majesty's commands in communicating to the Prince of Cobourg and to Prince Hohenlo the dispatch which I received on Friday, and I trust that your Majesty will be pleased with my success.

Though I am afraid little or nothing can be done on the side of West Flanders yet your Majesty may depend upon it that no opportunity whatsoever of annoying the enemy shall be missed by me, and in consequence your Majesty will find by the dislocation of the winter quarters that a very considerable body of troops are
cantoned within nine miles of Courtrai in order to be ready at all times to take advantage of anything which may arise.

Your Majesty will long before this have seen by my letter to Sir James Murray that the Landgrave of Hesse Darmstadt has consented to his troops being employed in the Vende`e, so that I trust and hope that none of the British regiments under my command will now be taken from me. The Hessian regiments which are destined to be embarked are already quartered at Ostend and Nieuport in order to be in readiness the moment the vessels are prepared to receive them.

I had intended to have left the Darmstadt troops in cantonments round Courtrai till the Cassel troops were embarked, as there is not room enough near Ostend to place any more troops there, but I am afraid I shall be obliged to remove them to Ipres, as they begin to desert so fast that they must be confined in a fortified place.

I have appointed Colonel Sporken to come to me tomorrow morning in order to converse with him upon a number of points. I am exceedingly happy that your Majesty has sent him over as it will save a great deal of time.

I am just arrived from Bruges upon Frederick's having wished that I should remain a few days with him. I therefore shall stay here till next Tuesday when I return to my Regiment. I was yesterday presented to it, but only to the Officers, as my own Company has so many sick that I was obliged to put off my seeing it till another time. In general it is amazing the number of sick the different Regiments have; mine has very near five hundred. It is a kind of a fever which the men get, and which pulls them immediately so down that it is a
long time before they can recover their strength again. They are well quartered in barracks which upon the whole are pretty good: there are 18 men in a room, but that cannot be helped for the citizens are all free: wherefore no soldiers can be quartered in their houses. The town is very large and monstrously dirty, the streets very narrow, and no place for people on foot to walk. This renders it very disagreeable. The horses your Majesty was so gracious as to give me arrived last Tuesday, and in perfect health; the groom is to return by the next packet boat which sails on Thursday. The Field Marschal returned last Friday from Mons where he had been to see Prince Coburg. General Mack is expected next weeck at Brussels, from whence he is to come to the Army to take the post of Adjutant-General. Ernest is very well; he is with his Regiment almost every day, but he comes back at night for Bruges where he is quartered. This day is the first day that it has snowed; it is exceedingly cold, but I believe very good, for it will be of great service for the recovery of the men.

note.value: 1032 THE DUKE OF YORK TO THE KING

text.p: As the time approaches when, according to the plan of the campaign, I am to move from here with a part of the troops in order to form the army upon the right of the Prince of Cobourg, I think it my duty to ask your Majesty's orders concerning the Hannoverians.

It was your Majesty's intention while I was in England that they should form a part of the corps I am to take with me, but I am sorry to say that the sickness which has prevailed so long in the Infantry continues still in such force that I have thought it expedient to ask Count Walmoden's opinion concerning the possibility of their being immediately employed upon active service. Enclosed I transmit it to your Majesty, by which you will see, Sir, that there is only one Brigade of the Infantry who were able to serve, and that the rest must be left back till such time as they are recovered. The Cavalry are in perfect good order and therefore I mean certainly to take them. It therefore now depends upon your Majesty's orders whether I am to take with me such part of the Infantry as is fit to serve at present, or whether I am to leave the whole of the Infantry back till such time as they are completely recovered and then move them forwards and send the Hessians back.

There is another point concerning the Hannoverians upon which I must beg leave to trouble your Majesty, which is, that there may be some arrangement taken about their being obliged to cook, and being supplied regularly with meat. I am sure that the want of these arrangements is one of the principal causes of their sickness; besides that, should we succeed and move forwards into France, it must be considered that the country we are to act in is completely eat up, and that if we do not take the precaution beforehand of supplying ourselves with meat &c. the troops must starve. I have talked these points fully over with Count Walmoden who thoroughly agrees with me, and I have desired him to lay these points more fully before your Majesty.

I trust that your Majesty will pardon the liberty I have taken of mentioning these things concerning the Hannoverians, but it is owing to my sincere regard for them and to my zeal for the good of the service.

Permit me to take the earliest opportunity of congratulating your Majesty on the entire submission of the Island of Martinico to your arms. I look upon myself as peculiarly fortunate in having been able to reach this before the trenches opened on Fort George (late Fort Bourbon), the principal fortress of this country, having thus been able to follow the progress of the siege from the very commencement of the first battery.

I beg to repeat to your Majesty the assurance of my warmest gratitude for the high honour conferred by you upon me in appointing me to a command in the army under Sir Charles Grey. I was fortunate enough to be named by the Commander-in-chief to take possession on the 23d, at the head of the Grenadiers, which brigade I am posted to, of the gates of the fortress, and I am at this moment returned from attending the ceremony of the French Garrison laying down their arms, and their embarkation in consequence.
With the most fervent wishes for your Majesty's welfare, and happiness, and the success of your arms, wherever they may go, I have the honour .

Here I am still and without any prospect of getting better, for though the arm grows thinner, yet 'till this moment I have no strength or power soever in it. The idea of being in this moment an invalid makes me very low spirited, & yet I am not able to alter it being totally unable to ride. The surgeons tell me daily it will be better, but God knows when this will take place.
We have been very unlucky. I am sorry to say many and many of your brave subjects, as well British as Hanoverian, have been sacrificed. Heavens grant things may soon change for we are almost knocked up, at least the Hanoverians. I never was so miserable as the last two days, knowing all my friends were in fire, and I hearing the cannonade & not able to serve; a man must be in my situation to feel this.

note.value: FROM THE CAMP AT OUDENARDE, 27 MAY 1794.

text.p:
Sense I last had the honour of writing to your Majesty the Hannoverians have changed their position. We were forced to retire last Thursday from our position behind the Espierre, on account of a village called Leers, which was in our left flank being taken. By this we were in danger of being cut off from Tournai as the enemy could get sooner on the pave` than we could so that by that we should have lost most probably all our artillery, as the pave` is the only road on which it can be transported. There was a bridge of pontons made in the night before over the Scheldt. This was intended for the transportation of the baggage, which is very much in the way on such occasions. I also received orders to retire with my Regiment and the Horse Guards over the Scheldt. This was effected in good order with the alteration that one Battalion of the Guards remained on the pave` for to cover the retreat of the rear guard: and that when that came up it was also to come over the bridge which then was to be taken up. This however was impossible to be effected, for the French advanced with such force that the Battalion was forced to retire on the chausse`e; & as we had waited to the last moment for it, we could only cut through the pontons to hinder any artillery coming over; & then retired as the enemy already begun firing with grape: however, I was so lucky as not to have a single man of the Battalion wounded; except the first Sergeant of the Artillery who was killed with a rifle. I unluckily lost one of the guns which had been drove into a ditch by the horses taking fright; this broke the axe, & therefore there was no possibility of saving it. The Regiments which passed over the river did not come any more into fire the whole day; but the other column which General Busche commanded remained
in it till 9 at night. They continued retreating till before Pont a` Chain, a village on the right of the great camp before Marquain: here they formed & a most violent fire of small arms toock place; they were forced again to retreat behind the village, which post they kept. My regiment, or rather the Battalion which had retreated down the pave`, tried three times to storm the village but without effect: at last the Brigade of the Line commanded by General Fox arrived: and after one general discharge of musquetry stormed the village and toock it. They were supported by the Hannoverians, who were almost knocked up, having been above twelve hours in fire during six of which it was so strong that, according to the opinion of those who have served in the Seven Years War, there was not so heavy a one during the whole last war. The English stormed with their accustomed bravery; this Brigade had particularly distinguished itself in the retreat on the 18th when the 37th attacked a French column & forced its way through it. The loss of the Hannoverians is not very considerable, considering the fire in which they had been. Most of the wounds are not dangerous, as they are from small arms; & these fired at a very great distance. The French must have lost prodigiously; the whole village was full of dead bodies, most of which were killed by our artillery, which has done wonders. According to the report of prisoners we have been attacked by four columns each consisting of about 16000 men; a proof of how very strong they are here. Most of the troops we had against us, were troops of the Line; & I believe this, the more, as they fought with such bravery. Last Friday afternoon the Hannoverians received orders to march off for Oudenarde: we marched the first night to Pots, & the next day toock our camp on the heights behind the town: I hear we are to change it this afternoon; & are to fall back with the camp, as the heights are to be fortified: I hope we shall have here a few days rest, for the men are quite knocked up with the fatigues they have undergone. Certainly the service we have had these last six weeck, surpass by a great deal what we had in the last campaign. I have sent to the Field Marschal the lists of what Captains Wangenheim and Jonquieres have expended in England. I could not trouble your Majesty with this, as I am sure that the Field Marschal will report it to you. I must beg pardon for having written so long a letter; and conclude with .

note.value: 1097 THE KING TO THE DUKE OF PORTLAND

text.p: Mr. Dundas yesterday acquainted me that the Duke of Portland, if I had not proposed his acceptance of the Lord Lieutenancy and Custos Rotulorum of Middlesex, would have wished to decline it in favour of the Marquess of Titchfield; this struck me so much as an highly advantageous method of bringing a young man of quality into a line the most useful to himself as well as the public if he zealously turns his attention to the police of the county and capital, that I authorized Mr. Dundas to desire the Duke of Portland to stop the Commission of Lord Lieutenant and have another made out in favour of the Marquess of Titchfield; but least any delicacy should have prevented the Duke from taking any step till he heard personally from me; I take this method of expressing my thorough approbation of the idea of the Marquess of Titchfield's being appointed Lord Lieutenant and Custos Rotulorum of the County of Middlesex, and directing that the instruments for that purpose should be prepared.

Understanding your Majesty has expressed a surprise at not having received any letter from me for some time, I hasten to recall myself to your gracious memory and explain to you the cause of my silence. Indeed, was I not assured this from authority I should not even now venture to trouble you, Sir, understanding that all correspondence with your Majesty's family was forbid me. However erroneous my conduct may have been, your Majesty will I trust not think my heart so perverse as to be capable of forgetting the various kindnesses you have constantly shown me even during my last stay in England. It was a principle of duty that kept my pen from tracing to you, Sir, my feelings on the occasion. Painful in the extreme was it to me to be left so entirely destitute of any friend or adviser, but as I understood it was your Majesty's wish that none of the family should write to me, it seemed also an order for me to correspond with none, which I silently submitted to. Private interests, however they may hurt my feelings and wound my heart, were never such as to make me forget for a moment what I owed to my father and Sovereign. That my situation is pleasant I cannot say. Futurity may perhaps shine more propitious than the present awful moment. My confidence in religion and my firm wish to be an honest man can be my only occupation now. Vivacity of youth may make one commit excesses, which it is, in cooler moments, our duty to repair as much as lays in our power, and I trust too much in your Majesty's good heart to fear a moment you will require of me anything but what is right. Any sacrifice which my conscience and honour allow, I am ready to make. Therefore I hope your Majesty will please to let me know through some channel (if you still intend to debar me the satisfaction of one kind line from your own hand) what your intentions may be. The very retired way in which I now live will I trust convince your Majesty of the sincerity of my sentiments.

With the warmest prayers for the continuance of your Majesty's health and happiness, I have the pleasure of subscribing myself once more (if your Majesty forgives me), your fortunate son and dutiful subject.

note.value: 1186 LETTERS FROM THE KING TO EARL SPENCER

text.p: As I perceive by the note from Earl Spencer in answer to mine that he concurs in my opinion as to the safest method of addressing myself to Earl Howe, whose health in the present moment is clearly not such as he could safely undertake a Winter cruise, I shall not fail to form my letter to prevent his retiring at present, and I am certain I can put his continuance at the head of the Channel Fleet in a light that will secure his taking the part which on many accounts I think highly necessary. As soon as I receive his answer I will communicate it to Earl Spencer that he may speak more positively to Lord Bridport, whose conduct will be highly absurd if he refuses to serve, and I confess, however I may think in general well of his nautical abilities, I do not look on them as superior to those of Vice-Admiral Cornwallis.

The letters from Vice-Admiral Hotham show the necessity of French ships of the line and frigates when the other services will admit of it . The Lowestoffe and Ballet being safe at Tunis is highly agreeable after the unpromising report of Captain Middleton.

Your Majesty's gracious letter of the 3d of this month I received at Ibbenbuehnen the day before I marched for this village, which prevented me returning you sooner my thancks for it. I certainly should have wrote from Munster, but as everything was quiet I would not trouble you with a letter, particularly as I had just wrote when we retreated from Holland. God knows this campaign has been a sad one, particularly the last 3 months of it. The fatigues we have undergone are very great indeed if one reckons the inclemency of the weather, and the more disagreeable as they have not helped anything. We have enjoyed very little rest this winter. I was exactly with my Regiment four weecks at Munster, & then marched into cantoonments which are very bad in this country. I am at this village since last Friday with my Regiment, & the rest of my Brigade, consisting of 3 Battalions & a Regiment of Cavalry, are cantooned in the villages round this. I am here in the second Line as a soutien for the first in case of an attack of the Embs, but hitherto everything is quiet. I can assure your Majesty that I never can thanck you enough for having let me remain this winter with the Army, as it is the greatest comfort in the world to have shared all hardships with the men; and now they are over I would not have missed them for anything. My Regiment is now beginning to get very sickly; this is the consequence of the severity of the last campaign: however, I hope that in a short time I shall get a great number of the convalescents. The worst is, the Hospital is so far off that it lasts a long time before we can get the men back. The weather has since some days grown milder, but the ice is still not yet gone. The roads here are schocking, much worse even than those in Holland, which is saying a great deal. It is with very great difficulty we can get on our artillery, and if the rainy weather sets in I do not know how we shall get on our guns.

note.value: 1231 THE KING TO THE PRINCE OF WALES

text.p:
I have purposely avoided answering your letters of the 9th of last month delivered to me by the Earl of Jersey, as well as that brought to me by the Duke of York of the 24th till the arrival of the Princess
Caroline, whose amiable qualities will, I flatter myself, so fully engage your attention that they will divert it from objects certainly not so pleasing to the nation.

There cannot be a doubt that the English do view with a jealous eye any decided predilection in those on or naturaly to mount the Throne to military pursuits, and I certainly feel the force of that opinion as strongly as any one. This for a long time made me decline granting you the Commission of Colonel Commandant of the 10th Regt. of Dragoons, and at last ordered it to be prepared on the solemn assurance of those you had employed to name this request, that no higher rank was meant hereafter to be claimed from it, and that the application arose alone from your desire of being employed in forming that regiment, and in going with it to camp, which you could not do without some military rank. I then declared from real affection for you, knowing that the approbation of the public ought to be your first object, that this Commission should not be the forerunner of a military career, and that I should certainly never grant any further military rank. When you therefore two years ago through Lord Amherst applied to be made a Major General, I declined it and mentioned to him what I had expressed on giving you the Commission of Colonel.

I own I am sorry you have again applied, but I cannot depart from what I have uniformly thought right. My younger sons can have no other situations in the State or occupation but what arise from the military lines they have been placed in. You are born to a more difficult one, and which I shall be most happy if I find you seriously turn your thoughts to; the happiness of millions depend on it as well as your own.

May the Princess Caroline's character prove so pleasing to you that your mind may be engrossed with domestic felicity, which may establish in you that composure of mind perhaps the most essential qualification in the station you are born to fill, and that a numerous progeny may be the result of this union, which will be a comfort to me in the decline of years, from thinking that both these Kingdoms any my German dominions may for ages continue governed by my lineal successors and on the same liberal sentiments of their ancestors, the intention of rendering their subjects prosperous and happy.

Having been informed by the goodness of the Queen of Naples that a messenger is going to England, I profit by the occasion for to write to your Majesty, being sure that my letter will neither be lost or opened. Encouraged by the very gracious and friendly letter I received from your Majesty about two months ago I most anxiously look forwards for the termination of an affair which so intimately concerns the future happiness of my life, and which may approach me nearer to you, Sir, than I have been for a great while. It would be improper in me to adopt any measure 'till informed of your Majesty's pleasure, therefore most ardently desire to know what plans you would wish me to adopt in order to bring matters to a happy and firm conclusion. Your Majesty's goodness and kindness towards me gives me great hopes of this fortunate event soon taking place. My petition now is that some method may be pointed out to me, for at present I am totally at a loss to know how to act. The happy union of the Prince of Wales which is so intimately connected with your Majesty's felicity, and of course that of the country, will I hope plead somewhat in my favour, and in consequence give me more particular reason of rejoicing in the event. What I have suffered has been great indeed, for though imprudent, I trust you do not a moment doubt of the honesty and warmth of my heart. Had other circumstances taken place, my rank and my situation might have made me pretend to higher employments. Now totally without ambition, without any pretension whatever, my desire is to see myself quietly and happily settled, which cannot be the case, as long as I do not enjoy the good opinion and protection of your Majesty, as also that of the whole family. Should you ever want my services, as have wrote to you, Sir, before, feeble as they may be, with pleasure will I come forwards in whatever way may be most agreeable to your own intentions, desiring nothing so much as to prove to your Majesty that my attachment to your person must be ever unalterable, both from the ties of consanguinity and gratitude. Before I conclude, Sir, allow me to congratulate you on your late birthday. Though in a foreign country
you may be assured no one felt more warmly the day, nor desired more to do honour to it than .

note.value: 1269 THE DUKE OF YORK TO THE KING

text.p: In consequence of the great scarcity of corn, I beg leave to suggest to your Majesty if you would not be pleased to approve of a general order being given out to the troops not to wear hair powder till further orders. I am sensible that this will be but a trifling saving in the consumption of flower, but it would have at the present moment a good appearance.

I have the honour likewise to report to your Majesty that Mr. Pitt expressed to me yesterday in the name of your Majesty's Ministers a great desire that the cavalry round London should be augmented as soon as possible, as the appearance of intended riots increased daily. Orders were therefore sent last night to the Greys to march from Barham Downs to Dartford, to the 1st Dragoon Guards to march from Lexden Heath to Romford, to the Inniskillings to move from Peterborough to Barnet, and to the 11th Light Dragoons from Lavant Camp to Kingston, which I trust will meet with your Majesty's approbation.

I was informed yesterday that it has been found necessary for the Tower detachment to be considerably augmented. Should therefore the duty be found too severe for the Guards it would be easy for the 11th Light Dragoons to take the Hampton Court duty.

I have not ventured to write to your Majesty for fear of having incurred your displeasure by my having asked for leave to return to England: nothing but the anxiety I am at present in can make me importune your Majesty with a fresh demand. You may recollect, Sir, from the unlucky wound I received last campaign, my left eye was merely weakened, but now, Sir, instead of its being recovered, so far from that, I am in the horrid apprehension of losing it, the greatest of evils. I cannot describe to your Majesty how amazingly melancholy & low spirited this idea makes me. I have written to my friend Price as he always took so much interest in my misfortune, and have begged him to speak with Dr. Wathen. Perhaps, Sir, by returning home, & by taking great care I may recover my sight. Your Majesty's gracious and fatherly behaviour to me during my stay in England makes me hope that my humble request may be granted.

The letter I have the honour to address your Majesty this day is the most painful one I ever recollect having wrote in my lifetime. The sole conviction of its being my duty gives me a courage on the occasion which nothing else could, for it is a most hazardous undertaking.

Upon the manner these lines are received by your Majesty depends my future happiness, all my future prospects of bliss; equally will they determine whether I am to lose the protection of my Sovereign, and the friendship of my father. What an awful, what an anxious moment is more easily felt than expressed! Many in my situation would seek to delay such an important decision. However, the anxiety that has so long preyed upon my mind and which I have in vain endeavoured to overcome, forces me to hasten the event, and therefore once more to submit my ideas to you on paper, and thus at least (be it even for the last time) unbosom myself to that heart that once loved me, that once esteemed me. This is not the first time I have applied to my father, these are not the first follies, the first errors of mine to which he has been a witness, and from which, with a compassionate, with a paternal hand, he has extricated me. Abused I have your goodness, Sir, and confess the little right I have at present to petition for anything; many others infinitely more deserving have a primary right to your protection, but Nature still (in spite of my conscience) points me the way, and to my father I again apply for relief.

Before I continue this subject which must be unpleasant to us both, but doubly
so to me from feeling myself in the wrong, I must entreat your Majesty to be convinced that whatever plan was conceived for the execution of that measure, which naturally has put me at such a distance from you, had its origin in me solely. No one is culpable, is reproachable for anything but myself. I might seek excuses in order to save myself, where they are the least expected, but scorn to accuse any one to exculpate myself; besides, passion might make me unjust. To you, Sir, I now apply for relief, and entreat you to consider the very dreadful situation I am in. On the one hand the fear and anxiety of offending your Majesty, on the other my duty to protect those who have suffered on my account, whom I love, and to whom I am doubly linked by an unfortunate child, who was doomed to misfortune from the very hour he was conceived. Consider, Sir, but for a moment my feelings, what I must suffer, and your Majesty cannot but pity me, for even a heart of stone would be moved. The conduct I have observed since the two last years that I am abroad will prove to you, Sir, I hope, my desire to submit as much as is in my power to your will. Many an unhappy hour have I with courage supported, flattering myself your Majesty would at last be convinced of my sincere attachment to your person, and make allowances for my imprudence. I am far from excusing myself, but now matters are once so far, I wish they were arranged in a manner conformable to the laws of the country, and at the same time in union with my conscience. The law must certainly be observed, it is by the strict adherence to the laws of the country that one can most contribute towards its felicity; but can a man of honour, a man of religious principles seek to deceive a harmless being by holding out a phantom, by making false promises and after having obtained his purposes abandon her because the law is in his favour? Can a man of feeling who, through an involuntary error, has become a father, forsake his child because the law is ignorant of his birth? With all dutiful submission to your Majesty, who is to protect the unfortunate companion of my misfortunes, and my helpless infant if I do not stand forwards myself? These, Sir, are questions that I can answer but in one way - There are insurmountable obstacles. Believe me (though I do not conceal my most sincere attachment to those who are concerned with me) my conduct has its sole origin in a firm reliance on the Almighty, and my sincere conviction that however erroneous it may have been before, the plan I am now following is the only one I can choose. Were I acting from passion, could my system be attributed to obstinacy I should be to blame, but religion, Sir, is my guide and adviser. I therefore once more most humbly and warmly petition your Majesty to come to some final determination, for the situation in which at present I stand is truly deplorable.
With every prayer for your Majesty's health and happiness, with every possible reliance on your paternal friendship and generosity, I have the honour .

The messenger's setting off for England renders me doubly happy, as it procures me an opportunity of writing to your Majesty. I should long before this have done myself that honour, but as I had nothing of any consequence to mention I was afraid of importuning you. I have lately been at Hameln for to see poor Wangenheim whom I found by no means well. His leg is a great deal better, but he suffers such horrid pains in his head that he can scarce
bear them, and this as often as ever he overheats himself. The physicians all say that nothing but time can cure him, & that several years must pass before he will be perfectly recovered. At present it is impossible for him to serve, and I am very much afraid he never will be able to make a campaign again, for the least change of weather and the least irregularity in his manner of living, which is the common case in time of war, bring on these headakes which render him incapable of doing anything. Nothing but a very regular life will do for him, and as he cannot find this in his present profession he will unluckily soon be forced to take his dismission, and it certainly would be a pity for a man of his age and parts to be living on a pension doing nothing: besides he wishes to be active, and I am sure he could still be of use to your Majesty in another line; I mean if you would be so gracious as to give him a Kloster Amt I will answer for his fulfilling his duty well. He has always been very fond of a country life, and as he possesses a very sound and upright understanding he certainly is very capable to do the duty of a Bailiff. You certainly can never reward a more worthy man, who has totally sacrificed himself for me, for he never would have been wounded had it not been for to save me. I am sure your Majesty will excuse the warmth with which I interest myself for Wangenheim, but I really have such particular obligations to him that I never can enough prove him my gratitude.

I must also ask your permission to lodge this summer at Mon Brilliant which is quite near the town. This great Castle in summer is quite horrid; the rooms in which I lodged are so exposed to the son that there is no living in them in summer; besides, as all the nobility go to their estates after the Birthday, the town is exceedingly dismal.
I will now not intrude any longer on your Majesty than only just to add that I ever shall remain .

Having just received from the Duke of York, by the February mail, a letter acquainting me with your Majesty's gracious goodness to me in promoting me to the rank of Lieutenant-General, I seize the first moment to offer you my humble thanks for so distinguished an honour. The summit of my ambition has always been, both in the line of my profession and in my general conduct, to merit your approbation. That my zealous efforts have not failed of success, this signal mark of your favour now permits me to hope. Nothing therefore is now wanting to complete the happiness which I experience from this hope, but the permission to throw myself at your Majesty's feet, that I may there learn from your own mouth that you have condescended to restore me to that place in your good opinion which I was so unfortunate as to forfeit by my imprudent conduct when at Hanover and Geneva. For this permission, Sir, allow me now to petition you. Eleven years are now nearly elapsed since I first quited the parental roof, in all which time I have been but once permitted to come into your presence. Actuated by sentiments of the truest attachment to your person, and by the most earnest wish to see you, I feel confident that if your Majesty will not condescend to grant my request, you will not be offended with me for having made it, or for having ventured to remind you of the length of my absence; nay, if I might presume to go still further, I would add, I almost flatter myself that you will lend a favourable ear to my humble solicitation.
It now remains for me only to add that every hour of my life shall be devoted to prove to your Majesty that I am not unworthy of the happiness of being permitted to subscribe myself .

note.value: 1398 THE KING TO THE DUKE OF GLOUCESTER

text.p: I return for the Princess of Wales the packet of letters which she sent to me through your channel on Monday last, as well as a few lines to her, both of which I desire you will deliver. I cannot wish to enter upon so disagreeable a subject as the disputes that led to this unhappy correspondence; too much heat appears from both, which tends only to farther accrimony. It is high time to put a stop to it, and if the Princess will, when he is at home, receive him with good humour and make him find that comfort not to be met with abroad, it may by degrees effect a better understanding. My son seems willing to live on terms of civility and good humour. You have told me she is willing to do so also. What then prevents its being attempted but some person of temper who, by stepping forward, might take the part of the absent, not the one spoken with; get materials for such an explanation as may prevent farther altercation. You seem, dear brother, the best person for this task, as you are equally related to both; the Princess seems to think no former etiquette necessary that frustrates her ideas of amusement; learn from my son what he expects, and bring the Princess to acquiesce to his ideas. Believe me, submission in a woman always secures esteem, she must obtain that before more can be expected.

note.value: 1410 THE DUKE OF CLARENCE TO THE KING

text.p: After the very gracious and confidential manner with which your Majesty has been so good as to treat me on the late unhappy occasion respecting my brother the Prince of Wales, I should have felt no scruple of communicating any wish of mine personally to your Majesty if I had not thought that by so doing I might subject your Majesty to some embarrassment. I am persuaded that to a person of your Majesty's character, truth and plain dealing only will be the most acceptable, and it appears to me most decorous to communicate my sentiments to your Majesty by letter.

I have learnt from a person nearly connected with Lord Spencer that from the state of his Lordship's health it is doubtful whether he will be able to continue long in your Majesty's service. It is natural for one who has served from his childhood in the Navy to wish to be at the head of this popular and favourite service, and I should think myself deficient in those generous sentiments which always have distinguished the House of Brunswick if my ambition did not lead me to a wish of standing first in my profession. I therefore presume to solicit your Majesty to be at the head of the Admiralty either as First Lord or in any other way which your Majesty may judge to be more proper and more becoming the son of a King of Great Britain. I freely express this wish to your Majesty because it is to you only , Sir, that I will ever be indebted for any situation in the Government of this country. I never have been and never will be a party to any intrigue with any of your Majesty's subjects, and though I shall ever respect those whom your Majesty shall in your wisdom think proper to appoint your Ministers, it is to your Majesty alone that as a son I ought to apply for any favour.

At the same time that I make this request I implore your Majesty to consult the good of the public service and your Majesty's personal affections on this occasion. I wish not to be the cause of the least uneasiness or embarrassment to your Majesty, and therefore I beg leave to add that whatever may be the result I shall be perfectly satisfied with your Majesty's determination, and that I shall continue to take every opportunity of proving myself to be with the utmost sincerity and filial attachment, Sir, .
P.S. If your Majesty should not think it right to comply with this request I should implore your Majesty to commit this letter to the flames and its contents to oblivion.

My dear Augustus, your letter without date brought by a messenger dispatched by Count Munster requires an answer from me. I therefore though reluctantly take up my pen, for however much I love my children, that must never make me one instant to lose sight of my duty as Sovereign of this country.

The letters of which you have sent me copies, which you have written to the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Lord Chancellor, with their answers, had been shown to me by them previous to their sending them to you. They have in their situations stated with every degree of propriety what it was their duty to write, therefore on this unhappy business little is necessary to be added by me, but that if you feel as you ought that the Law of this country has decidedly prevented the possibility of a marriage and that the farther continuance of any connection must cease, I in that event to set your mind at ease, shall not be adverse to making an allowance for the lady and support of the child.

note.value: 1436 THE DUKE OF YORK TO THE KING

text.p: I have the honour to transmit to your Majesty the monthly returns and weekly states, and to lay before you, Sir, for your approbation the recommendations for the vacant commissions. I must at the same time humbly beg your Majesty's pardon for not having sent these papers yesterday, but having had a very long conference with Mr Pitt and Mr Dundas and afterwards with the Duke of Portland upon several points, I was too late for the mail.

In the conference I had with your Majesty's Ministers, after due consideration it was determined to offer the command of the army in Ireland to Sir Charles Gray, but to my great surprise when I mentioned it to him this morning he has absolutely refused it, and in a manner which convinces me that he has completely made up his mind. He excuses himself upon the precarious state of his health, but thinks himself fully adequate to continue the command of the Southern District. Under
these circumstances it is very difficult to know who to recommend to your Majesty for the very important situation of Commander-in-Chief in Ireland, and the least objectionable arrangement in my opinion would be, to endeavour to persuade Lord Carhampton to accept of it.
